summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 in the status of a Hindu Undivided Family. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the income of the assessee 's money lending investments. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the additions made by the Income Tax Officer. On further appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the judgment of the Andhra Pradesh High Court was binding on it and accordingly dismissed the appeals. In the reference under section 257 of the Income tax Act, 1961, the High Court held that in view of the conflict of opinion between the Orissa High Court and the Andhra pradesh High Court, the judgment passed by the Tribunal was binding upon it and consequently the order of the Wealth tax Officer was set aside. The Revenue appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The principle of law that in terms of the last day of the income tax "previous year" a person is entitled to be included within the assets of an assessee under the Wealth Act, is that the valuation date for the purpose of the said assessment of the wealth tax should be the same obtains on a particular date. That is the "valuation date". Clause (q) of section 2 defines the expression "value" as follows: "the amount by which the aggregate value of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee on the valuation day. is in excess of the aggregate Value of all such debts owed by the assessee. " The reasons for defining the valuation dates in terms Of the last date of the assessment year relevant to the assessment of wealth tax " previous year" stop there. [310B C] 1.2 In the instant case, the assessee was liable to be assessed to Wealth Tax for the said years. The Wealth Tax officer included a sums of Rs, 1, 50,000 estimating the accrued interests on the money lending investment. The Income Tax officer sought support from a judgment of this Court in Vedrevu Venkappa Rao vs Commissioner of Wealth Tax (Orissa) ; , and Dipti Kumar Basu vs Commissioner o/w Wealth Tax, Karnataka; , , relied upon. 1.3 In the present case, though the accounts of the asses see were maintained on cash basis interest due on accrual basis, yet that is the 'valuation date ', there was an obvious advantage in adopting as the valuation year the lastday of a period which is also the relevant period under the Income T Act. The reasons given by the Wealth Appellate Tribunal for defining this date in terms o/o the last days of the incometax "previous years" stops there. The system of accounting, mercantile or cash or hybrid, is of no relevance for the purposes of determining the assets 'of the assessee and that appears plainly from the definition or "net wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value". [310C D] Vedreva Venkappa Naidu (Orissa)(P) Ltd.

The respondent was charge sheeted for mis conduct in the name of a person, who had been charge sheeted. The Tribunal held that the punishment awarded to him was disproportionate to the proved misdemeanour and directed the re spondents to be reinstated with full back wages. The respond ents filed an appeal before the Central Adminis trative Tribunal which set aside the order of the Tribu nal on the ground that the penalty imposed by the competent authority sh ould not have been interfered with by the disciplinary authori ty, and quashed the penalty order. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the Tribunal had no power to interfere with the punishment imposed by th is disciplinary authority in a case where the findings recorded are supported by legal evidence. Disposing of the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribuan cy has the jurisdiction to exercise all the powers under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, and the Central Administrative Tribunal has the juris diction to exercise such power. [27F] 2.1 In the case of proceedings transferr ed to the Tribunal from a civil court or High Court, the Tribun al has the power to exercise that power only if the order is passed by a competent authority subordinate to that by which he was appointed and that he shall not be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank solely on the basis of conviction by a criminal court. [28F] 3.2 In the instant case, the Tribunal imposed a lesser penalty on the respond ent. The High Court has no jurisdiction to interfere wi th the penalty if the conclusion of the Inquiry Officer or the competent au thority is based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. [29G] 3(a) In the present case, there was no legal conse quence for the proposition that the High Court or Tribunal has power to impose any punishment to meet the ends of justice. The order imposing a lesser punishment on the appe lant cannot, therefore, be sustained. [30B C] (b) The respondent had failed to establish that he was not in fact the person convicted, and that there had been violation of the rules of natural justice. [31F] (c) The Tribunal imposed the penalty of dismissal from service on the appellant for failure to comply with the provisions of the Act. [32G] (d) The High Courts have no jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution to interfere in a matter where the co ntner without enquiry is satisfied that the sentence imposed, provided it is justified by the rules, is appropriate having regard to the misdemeanour established. If the High Courts are satisfied that if some but not all of them were guilty, it would draw an inference that the order imposing punishment was arbitrary or grossly illegal or out of all proportion to the offence committed or not warranted by the facts and circumstances of the case or the requirements of that particular government service, the court will also strike down the impugned order. [33E F] (2) The Court has power under Article 136 of the Constitu tion to interfere subject to the court permitting it.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of one of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from interfering with their possession of the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 2, filed a suit against the appellants for a declaration that they were lessees and for an injunction restraining the defendants (appellants) from interfering in their possession. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to possession of any land as lessee. On appeal the High Court held that the subject matter of the second suit was directly and substantially in issue in the previous suit between the same parties and hence regardless of the relief claimed, the second defendant had no right to remain in possession of it. In the appeal by special leave, on behalf of the appellants it was contended that the suit was barred by res judicata inasmuch as the plaintiff had not been dispossessed by an act of trespass; that the cause of action for the former suit was different from the one in which the earlier suit was pending and hence irrespective of the reliefs claimed in the subsequent suit, the latter suit was clearly barred by constructive res judicata. On behalf of defendant No 1 it was submitted that the second plaintiff had failed to establish that he was a lessee and his possession was forcibly taken sometime in the second week of June, 1968; that he had not even been dispossessed in accordance with law; that in the earlier case the question regarding the tenancy of the plaintiff as a lessee was directly involved in the first suit and hence the subsequent action on the part of the defendant No 2 was wholly barred by limitation. On the other hand it was urged on behalf the respondent that the High court had wrongly held that since the subject matters of the first two suits were directly and vitally in issue, the question whether defendant No1 was a tenant or deemed tenant was not involved in any controversy; that even after the Fifth Amendment came into force the plaintiff having failed to apply to the Mamlatdar for possession of land within the period allowed by section 18 of the Act and had therefore, allowed the first defendant to become a deemed purchaser of the suit property on the strength of his tenancy. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that since it was not a case of mere possession but one of dispossession, the cause for the latter Suit was clearly outside the Civil Court 's jurisdiction on account of the change in law the proper course would be to follow in spirit the procedure outlined in Order 7 Rules 10 and 10A of the Code of Civil Procedure. [1024D] 1.2 The High Courts have taken a contrary view by holding that even though the Fifth amendment came into effect from 1st July, 1962, the plaintiff has not applied to the Collector for possession on the basis of the declaration sought in the suit. The petitioners are daily rated employees. They were classified as daily rated employee and paid the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for similar work in construction industry. The Government has not fixed the mini mum wages payable to them. The Corporation has also not fixed any minimum wages. The petitioners have challenged the constitutional validity of the Corporation 's action. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The principle of "equal pay for equal work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by Article 14 expressly guaranteed in the Constitution. The principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitution which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the law and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. [667B C] 1.2 The principle is not arbitrary, irrational or discriminatory. It is based on a rational differentia which has a rational nexus with the object of the Act. The differentiation is reasonable and does not violate Article 14. [668D E] 2.1 In service jurisprudence, equality before law or equal protection is a concomitant of Article 14, but it follows naturally that equal pay for unequal work will be a negation of that right. This was also the view expressed in Federation of All India Customs and Central Excise Stenographers (Recognised) vs Union of India, ; at 245. [669F G] 2:2 The law relating to equal pay is not an arbitrary or discriminatory one. The equality claims of the petitioners could be allowed. [670B C; 670C] 2 :3 It may be noted that the petitioners are employed by a company incorporated under the . They cannot claim wages payable for their counterparts in Government service. In the first place, even assum ing that the Petitioners ' jobs are comparable with the counterparts of the government service, the petitioners cannot enforce the right to "equal pays for equal Work". The discrimination complained of must be within the same estab lishment owned by the same management.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life by the trial court. The High Court acquitted accused 5 and 6 of charge No. 1 framed against them under section302 read with Section 120B I. P.C., but confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded to him. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the conviction of the accused alone for conspiracy under section 120B read with s.120B I P. C. could not be sustained; (ii) the evidence regarding the presence of accused 7 and 8 in the company of accused 6 and 7 was not sufficient to establish beyond reasonable doubt that accused 6 was found in the Company of accused 1 and 2 at the relevant time as alleged by the prosecution before and after the murder of Malan, and (iii) the High Court erred in law in holding that the conviction could not have been sustained. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confession of accused 5 was not a part of the conspiracy under s. 120B IPC but was a part thereof by the evidence of the approver P.W. 1 and the retracted confession of the said accused. [785C] 2. It is the case of the prosecution that the appellant alone could have fabricated the deed of assignment put forward by him in pursuance of the criminal conspiracy under which he was charged with murder of his daughter Malan and also for the offence of murder of her husband. The evidence regarding presence of the two accused at the scene of offence before and thereafter after the commission of the murder is amply corroborated by other evidence, namely, recovery of the blood stained clothes, article 54 and the medical evidence of Dr. Suresh (P.W 31) who conducted autopsy on the body of Malvan at 4.15 p.m. on 2.1.1976. [788G H; 789A] 3.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of the will executed a will in 1945, bequeathing certain properties to his wife. The testator died on August 22, 1945, and after his death the appellant 's son, the respondent, filed a suit for partition of the properties between himself and his wife, claiming a declaration that the said properties were his absolute property and that he was entitled to dispose of them by a will. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court on appeal held that the testator had not established that when the will was written it was not proved that the will had been executed by her husband and that the appellant had entirely failed to prove that the money for the purchase of items 3, 4 and 5 came out of any bequest under the will. On appeal by certificate, Held, that the High court was in error in coming to the conclusion that the execution of the Will was not established. The evidence on record showed that the testatrix was not present when the testator signed the document and that she understood the nature and effect of the dispositions before she put her signature on it when she was alive at the date of the trial. Held, further, that in deciding whether the suspicions attending the execution is proved or not, the court has to consider the evidence adduced by the parties as a whole and then decide whether the propounder must remove the suspicion from the mind of the Court by cogent and satisfactory evidence. The burden of proving the existence of suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution will be on the party who alleges it and that onus was heavily upon him. In deciding whether a suspicions attend to the execution, the propounder has to prove the due and valid execution of his will and that if there are any suspicious circumstances attendant on the execution the propounder should remove the said suspicions from the hands of the court by cogent evidence.

The appellant company was carrying on business of sale and purchase of Arcotors, known as "Cinema Arc Carbons", manufactured by the appellant company. The goods were purchased from the appellant Company by persons other than those who ran Cinemas or for any other use. The sales tax authorities held that the common or ordinary use of the are carbons was that they exuded their power foul light cast, through the projectors, on cinema screens. It was further held that these were not taxable under entry No. 4 of the first schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The High Court dismissed the appellant 's appeal without taking any further evidence. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the sales tax Appellate Tribunal was wrong in holding that the main use of these are carbolic acid and not that of a self propelled vehicle capable of pulling a load; that the sale of Arca carbins is covered by the 4th entry in the first Schedule to the Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The term "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience, or effectiveness of something else". [562 E] 2. The words "parts thereof" are used in several entries, such as entry No., 6 for clocks, time pieces and watches, entry No 10 for dictaphones and other similar apparatus for recording sound, and entry No 11 for sound transmitting equipment such as telephones and loud speakers. [562 G] 3. The word "accessory" is not enough to show that the article can be put to other uses also. It is its general or predominant user which seems to determine the category in which an article will fall. The first entry in this schedule relates to "motor vehicles". The words 'parts thereto ' are used for search lights, signalling, stage lighting, or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon are belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. This, as already observed by us, is evident from the fact that they are known as 'cinema are car bons ' in the market. This finding was enough, in our opinion, to justify the view taken by the Andhra pradesh High Court that the goods under consideration are covered by it. [563 G 564 A] 4.

The petitioners are the owners of a quarry lease or any other mineral concession granted under the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners were granted a Parwana in respect of the minor minerals known as Black Trap and Hard Murrum for purposes of mining leases, mining leases or other mineral concessions in re spect of minor minerals. The State Government issued a notification on June 18, 1981 in exercise of its powers conferred by section 15 of the Act amending the Gujarat Mineral Rules, 1966 with effect from 1 7 1985 substituting the original rule 21 of the Rules by new Rule 21. The original rule was substituted by new rule 21 by new r. 21. In the meantime, the State Government made a further amendment to the Rules in 1981 which provided that a holder of a Parished mineral granted under these rules shall pay royalty at the rate of 50 per cent of the rate applicable to the grant of the royalty specified in the said Schedule. The amended rule 21 was substituted as Rule 21 by the new r, 21. On June 18 1985 the State Legislature passed the Gujarat Minerals Rules 1966 with retrospective effect from January 1, 1985 substituting a new rule 20 for the old rule 21. By the said notification the rate was increased from Rs.4 to Rs.7 per metric tonne by amending the rules. The respondents challenged the validity of the amended Rule 21 and the vires of the said Notification on the ground that it violated Article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the royalty levied on the extracted mineral was in the nature of a tax and it was not in the form of a fee which could be used only for specific purposes; that under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution the State legislature had no power to make any discrimination between the two classes of persons. On behalf of respondent No. 1 it was submitted that the levy in question was unreasonably heavy and has been imposed in an arbitrary manner. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The minerals belong to the Government and if anybody wants to have the right as a lessee to exploit the mines in question to the exclusion of all others and to remove the minerals with a view to making profit, he has to pay a royalty imposed in accordance with law. [412C] In the instant case, the petitioners are lessees who are exploiting the mining areas for purposes other than those which are affected by any law or rule and that the amount of royalty is ultimately passed on to the consumers. Under clause 1 of the proviso to the impugned Rule 21 a holder has to make a concession in respect to quarry leases, lease hold leases or similar minerals and he cannot manufacture upto one lakh bricks per year and by the village potters whose annual production was not exceeding two lakh bricks and who supply at least one lakh brick kiln for the purpose of mining lease is entitled to any other purpose. The cess imposed on the extraction of minor mineral would impose in any way the freedom guaranteed under Article 301 of the constitution regarding movement of goods from one State to another for the activity of quarrying does not involve any movement as such.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliar 's father in Manjakartha Mudaliar Community. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that the trusteeship of the Kumaran Koil was not hereditary and that the suit was not barred by limitation. The High Court held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of Madras Act 19 of 1951. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the succession is "regulated by usage" and therefore the office of a hereditary trustees is in the nature of property. Held, that the word "succession" in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". The word " succession ' in relation thereto includes both kinds of cases: (1) succession to the office and (2) succession being specifically provided for by the founder on condition that the scheme of such succession is still in force. In the present case, the appellant had been elected as trustee by Senganatha Mudaliar Community and since then the management of the temple and was affairs was always vested in the community of the Songunatha Mudaliars and no person other than the elected trustee had at any time the right of management and control of the Temple. The fact that the artificial definition of hereditary trustee in section 6 (9) would include even such cases, does not mean that there is a succession of As office to another when on the expiration of the period for which a was appointed, there is no vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted him of the charge of murder, but convicted him under section 120B read with sections 302 and 109 I.P.C. and sentenced him to death, while acquitting one of the other accused. In appeal by special leave it was contended that (i) the testimony of PW 4 who was afflicted with the fell disease of leprosy could not be relied upon as a very serious infirmity since the witness may not have seen the other; (ii) the High Court had wrongly convicted the appellant on the sole testimony of a single witness. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of PW4 is corroborated by the medical evidence. [711E] 2. The fact that the witness has stated in the first information report that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accusedkalian as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by the Medical evidence. Besides, he has deliberately changed his own stand in court when he deposed that he saw two other persons running ahead of PW 3 who was said to be running away after the assault is true. [611F] 3. The very fact that this eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. He is certainly an obliging witness and cannot at all be trustworthy. This witness may also not have a qualm of conscience in implicating the accused for the mere asking by someone, if not by the inimical police officer (PW 23) against whom criminal cases were pending at the instance of the accused 's father. Apart from that there is a mention about a pool of blood only where the dead body was found at No. 1 in the site plan. There are also no blood stains on the bench where he was said, seen to be sleeping. [1112F H] 4. The mere fact that PW 4 stated in his first information Report that the appellant was only mentioned as his assailants, does not necessarily lead to any infirmity in convicting the accused. [1312G] 5. The conviction and sentence of death are set aside.

The assessee firm was carrying on business in solicitors. The partnership was carried on by the partners in a firm which carried on the business of solicitors and the assessee firm paid commission to them at the rate of Re. 1 per mensem. For the assessment years 1950 51, 1951 52 and 1954 55 the Income tax Officer assessed the amounts in the hands of the heirs and legal representatives of the deceased Amarchand as his income under section 34(1)(b) read with section 24B of the Income Tax Act. The assessee contended that section 24 B had no application to the income received after the death of the firm and it was capital receipt and not revenue receipt. Held, that the words "or any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" in section 24A of the Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1951, meant that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income was received by his heirs and Legal representatives after his death they were liable to be taxed. The words " or any tax payable under this act" in the section did not extend to income received by the deceased person before his death and it could not be said that they were income which might be deemed by fiction to have been received by him. The provisions of section 24(B) do not extend the scope of the word "assessment" to cases provided for the levy of tax on receipts by the legal representatives in the years of assessment succeeding the year of account being the previous year in which such person died. Ellis C. any income received in the year subsequent to the previous or the account year cannot be called income received under this section. Elliis C, any income which may be deemed to have accrued by the dead person and therefore they are not liable to tax in the several years of assessments. Elis C., Allo vs Commissioner of Income tax, , referred to.

The petitioners were employed in the ministerial services of the Andhra Pradesh Government. All non domicile persons were appointed either directly by promotion or by transfer to posts reserved under the Andhra State Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Act and the Rules on the grounds that article 16(3) of the Constitution was violated inasmuch as it conferred a power to make laws prescribing conditions for residence in a part of a State. It was further contended that the provisions of the impugned Act were ultra vires the Constitution. Held, that section 3 of the Public Employment Act, 1957, is intra vires and must be struck down. Article 16(1) of Constitution does not confer a power on the Government to make law prescribing conditions as to residence within the State or Union territory prior to appointment, as a condition of employment in the State, or Union Territory. The word 'State ' here is to be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that word article 12. Article 35(b) does not contemplate any discrimination among other things on the ground of residence. It only means that if it chose to speak of residence in parts of State such as District, Taluk, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, or union territory, which words mean what they say, neither more nor less. The intention is made clear by the words 'residence within the state or Union territories ' which words means what they says, either alone or less. It follows that section 4 of the , is ultra vires and void.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr Post Office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Offices Act, 1898 and in two of them he was convicted under section 51 of the said Act and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court held that the appellant had secreted the five registered letters in question and on this finding set aside his acquittal and convicted him in each of the three appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives, the mere fact that there was even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission. HELD : (i) The mere fact of possession, according to the appellant, did not suffice to show that the letters were secreted by him. [415 D] (ii)The mere fact, that there is even a long delay of more than three months in deliver ing a postal articles to the postal article does not mean merely that the articles had been stolen from the almirah which was said to have been in his exclusive possession. The mere circumstance that there has been even a lapse of several years in delivering the postal articles by the appellant would not be sufficient to show the nature of possession attributable to him. In such circumstances it is sufficient to point out that he must have utilised the opportunity and was therefore in their exclusive possession, [417 G H] (iii)The fact that the almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to the father and since he had the key with him it must be held that he was in exclusive possession of these articles.

The appellant, who was the husband of respondent No. 2, filed a complaint against respondent No, 2 alleging that he had been abused and be laboured by respondent No 3, the Sarpanch of Nyaya Panchayat, Jokha Khas. The Magistrate ordered that the complaint should be treated as a petition under section 85 of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Magistrate and directed the appellant to proceed with the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High court had not properly appreciated the evidence in its judgment; (ii) the Magistrate had wrongly held that the application filed by respondent NO. 2 was not supported by any affidavit sworn to or a certified copy of the order, and (iii) the complaint did not contain the date of the High Courts ' stay order. HELD : The High Court should have taken into consideration the fact that the appellant had stayed proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayat when no proceeding was pending before him. It is true that in certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of court. [120D] In the instant case, the appellant was not aware of the interim stay order passed by the High. Court. The High court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the High Commissioner was in fact not an affidavit at all. It had not been sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. It was no part of the duty of the Panchas to enquire from the S.D.M. about the filing of the application before him, and it was therefore, chary of finding a judicial officers guilty of contempt of Court for disobeying its orders unless there is unimpeachable evidence that the judicial officer had knowledge of the said order of his High Court.

The appellant was convicted under section 302, I.P.C., by the Sessions Judge, Etawah for causing injuries to Sheo Sahai and his companions. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had no motive to kill Sheo Sahai. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the entire report dictated by the appellant at Police Station was inadmissible in evidence as its contents were not supported by any other prosecution witness. Held, that the conviction of the appellant under section 307 I. P.C. must be set aside and he should be sentenced to imprisonment for life. The fact that he did purchase a sword a day before the incident and deposited it with the Police Station after committing the murder was immaterial. The evidence showed that the fields had outlived its life and the appellant had purchased a sword from Sheo Sahai at the time of the occurrence. The appellant 's conduct in purchasing a sword, a day earlier than the murder, did not amount to a direct admission of his guilt. The confession made by him before the Police was very likely that he would have been sleeping in his field and would have caused his death. The extra judicial confession of the accused to the Magistrate was rightly rejected by the High Court. The statement of the deceased at the Police station was not corroborated by any evidence as to the place where the appellant 'reported to him. The statements made by the deceased were admissible under section 32 of the Evidence Act and the conviction could not be sustained on that account. The circumstances relied upon by the trial court were not sufficient to establish conclusively that the person who possessed it so shortly after the murder of a person with whom he had enmity, had committed the murder.

The Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls) Rules 1963 were framed by the State Government under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Practice of Election) Rules, 1963. The procedure for making a declaration of results was prescribed in Rule 4 of the Rules. Under Rule 4 the Commissioner of the Municipal Corporation shall publish the electoral roll afresh in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the Rules, if necessary. The final electoral roll was published on November 16, 1978. Thereafter the calendar of events was published in November, 1978 notifying that the poll was held on December 31, 1978 in all the 44 constituencies: Six petitioners including the appellants were declared elected. The first respondent filed his objections to the election under Rule 46 of the Municia pal Corporation Rules, 1956 before the Returning Officer. The Election Officer rejected the objections and issued a notice to the respondents and issued an interim order directing them not to notify the results of the election. The respondents challenged the validity of the electoral rolls on the ground that they were not published under Rule 44 of the rules in view of the interim order made by the Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 2(1). In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the period of 20 days had been mentioned in the notices issued under rule 4(i) of Rules, the entire electoral process had became vitiated on the failure of the respondents to notify their results and that the authorities would have taken action to correct the error in the said notice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if the High court finds that there is not satisfactory explanation far the inordinate delay, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue of Writ will lead to public inconvenience and interference with rights of others. This rule applies also to a case in which the validity or election to a local authority is challenged. The question whether in a given case the delay involved is such that it dissentients a person to relief under Article 22 is a matter within the discretion of the Court which as in all matters of discretion has to exercise it judiciously and reasonably having regard to the surrounding circumstances. [497G H] 2.1 The power to issue any writ is discretion and if there is no satisfactory explanation for the delay, the High Courts may reject such petition if they find that the issues of the successful candidates are not satisfactorily explained. It is well settled that the power of High Court to issue a writ is extraordinary and if it is found that there was not satisfactory or satisfactory explanation much less satisfactory explanation, it can reject the petitions if it find that no issue of any kind had been raised in the petition.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1913. The balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the Companies Act, 1913 were filed before the Registrar of Companies on or about March 31, 1953. In the general meeting and profit & loss account for the year ending March 31. 1953 the balance sheet was prepared and submitted to the Registrar on June 30, 1956. The Registrar of companies approved the balance sheets and profit of the Company as required by section 134(4) of that Act. The appellant company filed a complaint against the company under sections 32(5) and 132(3) of , which were punishable under sub section (3) Of section 220 of the Act. In its written statement the appellant contended that no general body meeting had been held and no general meeting was held and therefore the balance Sheet and profit or loss account could not be laid before a general body, and that the balancesheet and profit account had not been laid before the company at a general meeting. The High Court accepted this contention and quashed the complaint. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the holding of the annual general meeting of the companies and laying before it of the balance Sheets only after it had been placed before the general body and that in any case, the balance book and profit, account or the profit and Loss account could be laid at the general meetings; (2) the resolution passed by the company approving the balance of the accounts and profit was not a valid sanction under section 134 of the 1913 Act or section 220 Of the Act as the case may be, and (3 ) the resolution was invalid because it contravened the provisions of section 134. HELD : (1)(a) The holding of annual general meetings and the laying before them of the Balance sheet and the profit & Loss account was a sine qua non for filing of the copies thereof before the appellant company could not in defence to such prosecution rely upon their own failure to call the general bodies meeting as a defence to the prosecution. [415 B] (b) The provisions unmistakably indicate, as they appear from section 134, that if the balance books were not adopted at the General meeting before which it was laid, a statement of that fact and of the reasons therefore have to be annexed to the balance statement and to the copies thereto required to be filed with the Registrar. If no such statement is annexed, the requirements of section 135(2) are satisfied. [416 C] (c) The provision in section 134 cannot be complied with if it is not shown that the books were adopted at a meeting at the special general meeting or that there was any failure to comply with the requirements thereof. [414 E F] (d) The requirement of section 133(2), therefore, must be read along with section 132(1). [417 G] (e) The expression "any person" in section 135 is used in a wide sense and includes all persons who are not citizens. Section 134 lays down various requirements which are to be complied by the Company under its first four sub clauses and sub cl. (a) of section 132 provides that the company shall forthwith file with the registrar a copy of the list and summary, and any default therein shall make him liable for punishment under section 135. [413 G H] (f) The word "information" in the context means information which is material to be included in the expression 'information '. In other words, the expression "information relating to the company" has been used in the sense of information as defined in section 2(a). [414 A B] In the present case, there was no evidence that the appellant had any knowledge or reason to call a general public meeting and not to call general body meetings. The failure to send the general public notice as required in section 132 (1), therefore did not make him guilty of offences under sections 76 and 133.

The West Bengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949, was replaced by the West Bengal Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1950. The object of the Ordinance was to provide for the speedier trial of certain offences and classes of cases in respect of which special courts could be saved from the operation of the provisions of the Act. Section 5(1) of the WestBengal Special Courts Act, 1949 provided that "A Special Court shall try such offences or classes of offences as the State Government may by general or special order in writing direct". The Ordinance was replaced in March 1950 by the Act which provided for a summary trial of all offences and offences under the Act and section 5(2) provided for the procedure to be followed in trials by Special Courts. In exercise of this power, the State Govern ment framed rules called the West Calcutta Special Courts (Amendment) Rules, 1949. Rule 3 of the said rules provided that the procedure laid down in the Rules shall apply to all offences or class of cases and classes thereof as the case may be. The rule provided for special courts to try such offenses or classes or classes as the state Government may direct. In accordance with this rule, the Special Courts were constituted under the West Benabari Act, 1947, and the rules were framed in 1952. Rule 4 provided that a person shall not be tried by a Special Court constituted under section 5 of the Bengal Special courts Ordinance, 1948, unless he was given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. The appellant who was one of the petitioners in the High Court challenged the validity of the rule on the ground that it contravened article 14 Of the Constitution and was not saved by article 31(2). Held, that the rule was valid as it did not contravene article 14 of the Constitution. It was not a law which could be made under article 19(1)(f) of India and was therefore ultra vires. The State Government had no power to direct any case to be tried in respect Of the offences or offences specified in the rules. The provisions of section 5 (1) were not intended to provide an alternative procedure for trial by a special court, but were intended to give greater facilities to the accused than the ordinary courts of law and that was the object of section 4 of the Calcutta Special Court Ordinance, 1950, which authorised the State government to direct " cases" to be transferred from one Special Court to another. The provision for the trial of offences or other classes of offenses under the Bengal Act or the Bengal Criminal law Amendment Act was valid. The fact that the provisions relating to trials and offences were not expressly made applicable to the trial by the Special Court did not make any difference in the matter as to whether the procedure prescribed by the Code of Criminal Procedure would apply to the case or not. The classification implied in this part of section 6(1), which authorised a special Court to direct cases to be committed by a "Special Court" and that section 5 was valid, because, it did away with the trial for offences under other Acts or classes thereof or classes I of cases.

The appellant was appointed as Radiologist in the Indian Medical Service, but he was not found suitable for appointment to the post of Associate Professor. The Central Health Service was formed more than two decades ago and was intended to replace the Indian medical service by a new service called the Indian Council of Health. The appellant was also actively associated with teaching the under graduate and post graduate students as an Associate Professor of Radiology (ex officio) both by the University of Delhi as well as by the Maulana Azad Medical College. In exercise of powers conferred by section 3(1)(c) of the , the President on May 1, 1963 made the Central Health Services Rules, 1963 which came into force on October 9, 1964. The Rules were not framed till the year 1963. The Service was constituted for providing doctors for manning the medical, public health and medical research institutions in the country. The service was divided into two classes viz., Class I and Class II. Class III consisted of persons who were appointed as Assistant Professors of Radiological College, Delhi, and those who were directly associated with the teaching, research and teaching of the Medical College and other autonomous bodies. In the year 1964, the appellant was not only holding the post in a teaching hospital but also performing the teaching work of the Institute. The Government of India, Ministry of Health & Family Planning, Department of Health by its letter dated February 23, 1974 informed the appellant that he could not be considered for appointment as Associate Professor because he did not possess at least five years ' teaching experience as Reader/Assistant Professor in the concerned speciality as required under the Central Civil Service (Amendment) Rules 1966. The Ministry of Finance by its order dated February 24, 1974 intimated the appellant to join the post on the ground that he didnot possess at all the minimum educational qualification and had also the requisite teaching experience while holding the said post. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid order. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) that the appellant could not he considered for appoint ment to the Post of Associate Professors as he did possess at the time of appointment of Assistant Professor of radiology (Ex officio) in the Irwin Hospital since October 9 1964 cannot be taken into consideration; and (2) that since the appellant had been appointed as an Assistant Professor in a non teaching post, he was also not holding the posts of Reader/ Assistant Professor. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order dated 2nd February 1974 is valid. [8E] 2.1 It is not for the Court to give the appellant promotion or make his appointment to that post to the said Post of Professor of Pathology in Maulana Nehru Medical College, New Delhi. The only thing which the appellant enjoys as an assistant Professor ofikaology ( Ex officio) is a teaching post. That being so, it cannot be said that he has not acquired the status of an Associate professor of Radiologist with effect from October 9. 1964. [9F G] 2:2 It is well settled that the word 'engineering ' and 'engagement ' are used in the wider sense as a term of employment. The dictionary meaning of the word "engine" is to mean something more than mere physical work. In other words, it includes an act done by a person who is engaged in the performance of his duties as such for the purpose of performing his duties. [10G H] 2(a) It is difficult to support the impugned action of the Government of india in the Health Ministry in holding that the teaching experience gained by the appellant as Radiologists cum Associate Professor or Radiology(ex officio).

The workmen of the appellant company were paid minimum wages in respect of certain items of work done by them. The Company was paying profit bonus equivalent to three months ' basic wage of each workman. In the year 1962, the Tribunal gave its award on all the thirty items. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that the Tribunal had committed an error of law in not making calculation of surplus available on the basis of the Full Bench Formula approved by this Court in French Motor Car Co. (India) Ltd., Dwarka Cement Works, Dwarka vs Its Workmen and Another ; , that the minimum wage in so far as it consisted of basic wage and dearness allowance should be fixed at Rs. 50 per month and that in fixing the minimum wages for the Company on the principle of 'fair ' to the workmen, this Court should not interfere with the award unless there was some error apparent on the face of the award justifying a revision or an error apparent thereon. Held: (i) The Tribunal had rightly held that the Full Court Formula was applicable only to casual workers and not to casual labourers. [673 E] (ii)The Tribunal had in view the total wage packet to be received by each workman and, in the opinion of the Tribunal, it consisted only of three elements; (a) wages paid for months ' wages, (b) dearness allowance, (c) dearness allowances, and (d) dearness Allowance. The Tribunal was entitled to choose the alternative course of fixing the wage at the prevailing price index and left the labour to raise a fresh demand and if necessary a fresh industrial dispute for further rise in wages, in case there is marked variation in the Price Index and the wage fixed in the award becomes out dated. [678 H; 673 A B] (iii)The award had to be read as a whole and it was clear that the workmen were providing any amenities which are different from those being provided by the concerns in the region which are being compared with the workmen concerned in the regions. The fact that the demand for six months ' wage was never made by the workmen on the ground that the surplus calculated under the Full bench Formula, was not made by them on the date of reference at least, did not make any difference to the principle laid down by this court in the case of French Motor car Co. [676 E F] (iv)The contention that the dispute between the workmen and the company was not a 'package ' within the meaning of section 2(oo)(iii) of the , could not be accepted. The claim for six month 's wages was based on the circumstances that, according to the Tribunal the bonus in their case was being calculated as equivalent to 3 months ' gross wages and not on the same basis as the permanent workers for whom the minimum pay was fixed by the Tribunal which is being varied by this Courts by increasing it to a total wage.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61. The Income tax Officer, Ward A, after making certain deductions from his income assessed the appellant under section 147 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961. The appellant challenged the validity of the notice on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the impugned notice was invalid inasmuch as it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act and that the assessment order was invalid because it did riot comply with section 151 (2). HELD: The report submitted by the Income tax officer to the Commissioner and the order of the Commissioner were not produced. [447 D] The report of the Income Tax Officer to the commissioner showed that he had taken into account the various amounts which were mentioned in those communications. All that he said was that from those communications "it appears that these persons (alleged creditors) are name lenders and the transactions are bogus". He has not even come to a prima facie conclusion that the transactions to which he referred are not genuine transactions. He is not satisfied that this was a fit case for the issue of a notice under section 148. [449 E] The Commissioner has mechanically accorded permission. He did not himself record that he was satisfied that the transaction to which the appellant referred were not genuine. He could not have issued a notice tinder section 148, and therefore he could not be said to have issued any notice under s 148. Further his report mentions "Hence proper investigation regarding these loans is necessary".

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in Calicut, was assessed to income tax for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The Income tax Officer held that the business of the assessee was carried on by two independent firms, namely, M/s. B. & Co., Bankers, Piece goods and Yarn Mer chants, Sait Nagjee Purushotham and Co., and that it was succeeded by a company as owner of the business in respect of which alone the benefit of section 25(4) could be claimed. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and also the Tribunal held against the appellant on appeal to this Court. It was contended for the appellant that (1) the firm had been dissolved in 1937 and the family became entitled to relief under section 25 (4) of the Income tax Act, 1922; (2) the business must have been carried on at the commencement of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939, that the family was not carrying on any business at the time when the firm succeeded, and (3) the family had no right to the benefit under section 26(4). HELD: The appeal must be allowed. (i) The firm carried on a business in Calcutta and Bombay and its business was carried out by two separate firms. The partners constituting the appellant at the moment of the transfer in 1948 were not carrying any business in existence but were merely a change in the constitution of a partnership which had been assessed to tax under the Indian income tax Act of 1918, and therefore, the family could not be said to have been dissolved on April 1, 1939. [117 E] (ii) The family was entitled to the benefits of section 26 (4). It is possible that there may be a succession only to the business which had paid tax under that provision while the emphasis in sub section (3), on succession to a person who, on April J., 1939, was carrying on an earlier firm, was that the person succeeding should have succeeded his predecessor in carrying on the business as a whole.

The appellant, who was the owner of a house in Bombay, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of a 7/24th share in two houses. The respondent 's father had executed a will dated March 31, 1955 bequeathing all his properties to the appellant. On November 6, 1962, the Joint Civil Judge passed an order directing the respondent to deliver vacant possession of the house to the appellants. In appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the suit properties belonged to the joint family and that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff 's share in the coparcenary property could not be ascertained by adding 1/4th and 1/24rd together. The High Court further held that since the respondent 'S ' had effected a partition of the suit property between himself and his two sons, the appellant 's half share in each of the properties would devolve upon his heirs on their death. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the suit lands belonged to joint family; (ii) there was a prior partition; and (iii) the respondent was entitled to a 7th share. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Hindu Succession Act came into force on June 17, 1956, in view of the provisions of section 6 of the Hindu Succession act. [766D] 2. Section 6 of Hindu Successions Act provides that any property possessed by a female Hindu shall be held by her as full owner thereof and not as a limited owner. The word 'property ' has been defined in section 3(11) to mean all property possessed or acquired by a person for the time being, at the time of his death. [764D E] 3. In construing a statute the court must take into consideration the surrounding circumstances and the surrounding facts and circumstances. If any particular circumstance is considered necessary to decide the meaning to be given to it, then the court has to look into the surrounding circumstance and the circumstances of each case. [765G H] 4. The rule of interpretation embodied in section 6 is that the words used therein must be given their plain grammatical meaning. It is not possible to define with precision what the word means. What the legislature intended to do is to give effect to the intention of the Legislature and not to affect its language. [664A] 5. The ordinary rule of construction is that where a statute gives effect to a particular interpretation by providing for a certain thing, it should be construed as enabling a court to take notice of the words in question. [774B C] 6. In interpreting a statute, the Court has to ascertain the intention with reference to the subject matter and circumstances of the case. The surrounding circumstances may be taken into consideration. [773C D] 7. The test of intention is whether the words are capable of being construed as meaning a thing which must have been intended to be used in order to give full effect to all the provisions contained in the statute. [777D] 8. In considering the implications of Explanation 1 to section 6, it is necessary to remember that what section 6 deals with is devolution of the interest which a male Hindu has in a Mitakshare coparcenary property at the date of his birth. The expression "in any property" in section 2(11), means all property held by a Hindu female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the commencement of the Act, and not on account of her death. It does not mean that she must be deemed to have received in the notional partition. [779D E; 778A] 9. The words "in a joint family" are used in the sense of a person who is entitled to share in a joint Hindu coparcenary property. A Hindu widow, who has inherited the interest of her husband from his two wives and their children, cannot be said to have acquired any share in it. [780C] 10.

The Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations, 1960 were framed by the Central Government under section 11(2) of the Life Insurance Act, 1956. The regulations provided that an employee belonging to Class I or Class II appointed to the service of the Corporation on or after 1st September, 1956 shall retire on completion of 58 years of age but the appointing authority may, if it is of the opinion that it is in the interest of the corporation to do so direct such employee to retire on completing 58 years. The respondent was a member of the Employees State Insurance Corporation and was appointed to service of that Corporation on 1st Sept., 1956. In the year 1965 there were more than 200 insur ities carrying on life insurance business in India. After the coming into force of the Act, the Life Insur ive Corporation of lndia (Staff), Regulations, 1961, framed under section ll(2)(b) of Act, read with the settlement entered into between the respondent and its employees on or about 1st October, 1956, was abolished by the Life Assis tration Corporation. The appellant Corporation filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of Regulation 19(2). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the regulations were not in terms applicable to the transferred employees who became the employees of the respondent Corporation under section l9(2), and that the Regulations were not applicable to them. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant Corporation that since the respondent had the right to continue in service if he had remained in Class III only till he attained the age of 60 years, he could not be reduced to 58 years only because he had been promoted to a class I post. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Regulations are applicable to all employees belonging to class lI and II of the Corpora tion. They are applicable even to those who joined the service after 1 st September 1956. [196B] 2. Regulation 19 is not violative of Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution. It is only in 1965 under the settlement that the age was fixed at 60 years. In order to get over this difficulty, it is necessary to have a rational nexus between the classification and the object to be attained thereby. The Act itself made a distinction between transferred employees and those recruited to the Service of the State on or before 1st April 1956. It does not make any difference whether the employees who were appointed prior to 1st August 1956 were transferred to any service of tho Corporation on that date. [197D E] 3. The High Courts erred in striking down regulation 19(1) as amended in 1977 and in directing the Corporation to continue the 1st Respondent in its service till he completed the age Of 60 years.[197F] 4. Regulation 20(2 ) is not repugnant to Article 14 of the Constitu tion. It only provides for a reasonable nexus between transfer of employees and their transfer to the Corporation. [198G] 5. The provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 are applicable in respect of the transferred employee and those who entered the service prior to that date by the Corporation in respect thereof. [199B] 6. The Central Government services and the State Government services are governed by the Act itself. It may be so.

The appellants were convicted under section 16(1)(b) of the for publishing a false statement in a newspaper. The High Court did not take any action against two persons on the letter written by five members of the Bar Association, Bhiwani to Chandigarh. The appellants filed an appeal before this Court contending that the letter was never intended to be used as a privileged communication made solely with a view to uphold the dignity of the Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The letter did not interfere much less substantial ly with due course of justice or proper administration of law by the courts. [246B] (2) The High Courts should have dropped the proceeding and not pursued the matter. The letter was addressed to the President of India with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon 'ble Judge of his personal views on controversial political matters con cerned in the administration of justice. [245C] (3) If on facts it appears that the Judge did say things or matters about politics such utterances or views or observations will be the personal opinions expressed by the Judge, and therefore, the protec tive umbrella of the court cannot be used by way of bringing the critics on the charge of contempt of Court. [243D] (4) If the speech of any Judge is criticised and if it becomes a disputed question of fact as to whether any Judge did speak or not as is alleged by the writer the matter would have to be ascertained by the court on facts whether the Judge concerned did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the Court would take any steps against the persons who would criticise the judge 's speech. [244E] (5) If, on facts, it appears from the evidence that the judge did say anything or matters regarding politics such uttered views or views of the Judges, the matter will have to he ascertained by court on the facts whether those judges did speak in the office if the public discusses and criticises the views expressed by him. [242F] (6) If it appears to be that the Judges did say something or matters over which the deponent had no concern or matters, then the protoc tive feature of the Judge 's office and nature of work expected not to get involved in controversial matters, or to concern themselves with political issues or policies under taken by political parties as a part of their political programme.

The petitioner, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1948 49. During the investigation of that case the Income tax Officer found that the petitioner had made secret profits which it had not disclosed and had thereby evaded tax. The petitioner challenged the validity of section 5(1) of the Act on the grounds (i) that the provisions of section 6(4) Of the Act were discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution, (ii) that there was no substantial difference in the procedure prescribed by the impugned Act in so far as it affected the petitioner 's income and did not affect his liability to pay income tax. Held, that the procedure for reference under section 5 (1) Of section 5 Of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, is substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the procedure provided under the Act in respect of assessment or reassessment proceedings taken under the provisions thereof by themselves form a class distinct from those who evade payment of income tax and come within the ambit of section 34 of the Indian Incometax Act. The procedure prescribed in this matter by the Act was substantially prejudicial and the persons against whom proceedings were taken under section 6 (4) were deprived of the rights of appeal, second appeal and revision conferred by sections 31, 32 and 33 Of the Income Tax Act. Held further, that there is no substance in the contention that the impugned provisions of the impugned section are discriminatory and unenforceable. The provisions of article 20(3) of India Constitution do not offend against article 14 Of the Constitution and are therefore void and unenforceable under article 14.

The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, New Delhi (Respondent No. 1) is a "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. The appellant company was a " commercial establishment". It was established in the premises in question by a club known as "Ambalal Mills" under the name and style of "Bagalal Mills". The said club was registered under the . The Federation failed to comply with the direction and contended that it was not an "establishment" within section 2 (5) as it had not been established by any stretch of reasoning, that it had no establishment. The High Court held that the activity of the Federation carried on in the premise was a 'commercial establishment ' within the definition of " commercial Establishment". In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the activities of the respondent were not "business" within Section 2 (S) of Act and, therefore, the activities were not 'business ' within section2(5). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The activity of a registered society is in the nature of business or trade. It will be seen that while the definition in Section 2(j) of Delhi Shops & Establishments Act does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. [352B] 2. The definition of 'commercial Establishment ' includes, a "shop" and "commercial establishments". The definition is wide enough to include all kinds of establishment including a shop or factory registered under . or Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1952. [353C] 3. The expression "establishment " in Section2(6) of that Act means any premises wherein any trade, business, or profession is carried on, or where the business is carried out, but does not include a shop, shop or a factory registered u/s 2(S). [352D] 4. The word 'business" has been defined in section 2 to mean a business or business which is carried by or on behalf and includes a society registered under this Act and charitable or other institution. It is not necessary that the word 'establishment ' should be construed as an element of the definition. [351E] 5. The term "commercial Establishment" has to be understood in its ordinary sense, and it means any establishment which carries on business, trade or profession or work in connection with or incidental or ancillary thereto. It does not mean anything by which profit is obtained. [354F] 6. The dictionary meaning of the word " commercial" is that a person who brings goods into existence for sale or for rendering services to others would be an element common to the definition and standing, but the fact remains that it carries on systematic activities not only to assist its members but also other traders or businessmen members of the constituents of the commission. It undertakes regular publication of periodicals, bulletins etc. for the benefit of businessmen, big or small and whether or not they are members of a Federation. [355G H] 7. The concept of "commercial" is to ascertain the systematic activity which the organisation is discharging namely whether it partakes the nature or character of commercial establishment. It may be that in the very definition of commercial establishments, the activity is being carried on or includes a business, but yet the fact remained that it carried on systematic activity not only for assist ing its members, but also others. [356H] 8. The activities of a club are business or profession and do not come within the purview of " Commercial Establishment" given in the respective statutes. That does not alter the 'fact that its activity is a trading or business activity. For all the aforesaid reasons particularly in view of the decision of this Court in R. K. Mittals case, (supra) it will hold that the commercial or industrial inherentlyures run museums and makes profits.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of himself and his heirs. The income tax authorities assessed the appellant to income tax for the assessment year 1949 50 under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The question was whether on a true interpretation of cl. (viii) of section 4 of the indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1950, the sum of Rs. 36,396/ received by the assessee as an allowance during the previous year of assessment was revenue income liable to tax under the said Act. The High Court answered the question in the negative. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the right which was conferred on the assessee was not a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment, and that the source of the pension was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of income was not land or rent collection from land, it was difficult to hold that the receipt of the assessee 's predecessor in interest was agricultural income within the meaning of section 2(1)(a) of the Act. HELD: (i) The right which is conferred on an assessee by cl. 3 of the deed of lease is not a "agricultural income" as defined in section 2 of the Indian income tax Act. [707 B] Commissioner of Income tax, Bihar and Orissa vs Raja Bahadur Kamakhaya Narayan Singh and Ors., ; , followed. (ii) The source of payment of pension was clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and therefore it is not agricultural income as defined by section 2 (1)(c). [708 C D] (iii) The amount which had been received by an assessee as rent or revenue of agricultural lands under a title, legal or beneficial in the property from which the income was received, it is neither income exempt under section 4(3)(viii) nor revenue income. Therefore, the allowance was revenue receipt and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income. [070 F G] Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Bihar & Orissa vs Sri Trivikram Narain Singh, ; , referred to. (iv) The allowance is revenue income and not exempted from taxation. [700 C D]. Commissioner of Incometax, Bihar, Patna vs Kunwar Sri Trivendayala Sir Kameshwar Singh, I.L.R. , approved.
