The Karnataka State Transport Authority issued a notification under section 63(7) of the , authorising the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation to operate in any inter state route. The appellant State Transport Appellate Tribunal granted three out of eleven permits to the Karnataka state transport corporation, one permit to private operators and another permit to the other. The Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation filed appeals before this Court against the decision of the High Court. The Tribunal allowed the appeals and set aside the grant of three outgoings in favour of the Karnataka Road Transport Corpora tion. The High Court took the view that having regard to the rule of preference enunciated by the proviso to section 63 (7) the applications from the 'non preferred ' category had to be excluded as the number of applications from each applicant who were required to be given preference exceeded the number specified in the latter part of the notification. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that the view taken by the High Courts and the State Transport Tribunal was correct and that the true position was that on a correct interpretation of the proviso, the applications form for grant of permits were to be examined as application of any other private operator. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso to Section 63(1) for example provides that other things being equal, an application for a stage carriage permit from a cooperative society or a person holding a valid licence for driving transport vehicles shall be given priority over others. [1015B] 2. The expression 'preference ' occurring in section 47(1 H) of Chapter IV A of the Act is wide enough to include a registered co operative society and a person possessing a licence for drive transport vehicles. Section 47(l H) provides that where, in pursuance of an approved scheme, a State Transport Undertaking applies for a Stage carriage permit, a contract carriage permit or a public carrier 's permit in respect of a notified area or notified route, such permit shall be granted to the State Road transport Corporation by the State Government in a case where the said area or route lies in more than one region and the Regional Transport Authority in any other case. [1097C D] 3. The word 'preferred ' occurring under section 47 (1 H), however, does not mean, for example, like section 68 F(1). It is an inclusive definition of 'preferable co operative societies '. The words 'preparation ' and 'premise ' are used interchangeably. The context in which the word occurs in the proviso has to be understood in a broad and general sense. [1005C D; 1016E] Sher Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to. 4. In an application under Chapter IV, Corporation has to enter the arena like any other applicant, face the competition and come up to the level of other private operators intending to obtain stage carriage permits and then in respect Of the route in question claim preference.

The respondent purchased a business carried on by the appellant under the name All India Trading Company. Purushottam Raju was the sole proprietor of the business and had been assessed to sales tax in respect of his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the said business. The respondent 's contention was that the transaction was a sale of goods which were discontinued or the ownership of which had changed. The appellant contended that the State Government had no authority under section 19(1) and 19(2)(c) of the Act to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of the, business was constituted as the dealer liable to pay the tax in his hands. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Govern ment under section19(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) Rule 21A is ultra vires as it does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee; and (ii) Rule 22(c) is ultra rites. HELD: The rule making powers of the state Government under section 9 of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939 are beyond the rule made by the State Legislature either under section 10 or section 19 (2)(C) of Act. [665 B] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., ; , followed. Badrida Chetty vs C .I. T., ; and Badridah vs C I.T. (Central), Calcutta, ; , referred to.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Inspector General of Prisons, Saurashtra on February 2, 1955. He filed a suit for a declaration that the order of dismissal was illegal and void. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that there had been breach of article 311(2) of the Constitution as according to him there was no duty to supply a copy of the report of enquiry held against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts erred in holding that there was a breach of Article 311(1). HELD: (i) The question whether reasonable opportunity has or has not been afforded to the Government servant must depend on the facts of each case, but it would be in very rare cases indeed in which it could be said that the Government servants are not prejudiced by the non supply of the copy of a report of the enquiry held by the Enquiry Officer. The appellant is not concerned with the second contention but only with the third contention. [924 B C] (ii) The High Court erred in striking down the order as it was passed without giving any opportunity to the respondent servant to defend himself. It is true that the question whether a reasonable opportunity had or has never been afforded by the Government Servant must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each particular case but it will be in many rare cases, where a suit is brought by a Government servant for arrears of salary, the decree more properly falls under section 60 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act. [936 D E] State of Bihar vs Abdul Majid, ; , referred to. (iii) The words 'actionable wrong other than breach of contract ' in article 311 are wide words and include something more than torts, but even so where a claim for arrears is made on a ground which is referred to in cl. (b), the initial allocation of rights and liabilities made by this sub section shall be subject to such financial adjustment as may be agreed upon between the State (i.e., the Government) and the Government. [981 E F] In the present case, the appellant was not concerned in the second appeal but only in respect of a choice between section 60 and section 61 which lay down two broad categories. It was therefore not necessary to decide whether reasonable opportuni ty had or had not been given to the government servant to prove his innocence.

The appellants were the owners of a coal mine. The respondents filed a suit for possession of the coal and the appellant contended that the suit was barred by limitation. Held, that the onus of proof to establish knowledge on the part of the respondents beyond the prescribed time was on them and the suit must fail. The burden of proving knowledge on them is on the plaintiff who asserts a right and it may be, having regard to the circumstances of each case, that such a burden is on him to succeed in the plea of limitation. The onus is upon the plaintiff to prove that he obtained the knowledge of the fact from his father. The appellant gave evidence to show that the encroachment was prior to 1932 but there was no acceptable evidence on their part to establish that the respondents came to know of the removal of coal by the appellant or their possession of it. Held further, that in view of the provisions of section 3 of the Indian Mines Act and the Rules framed thereunder the onus is on a plaintiff who alleges a right, and it cannot be said that he has knowledge of such fact on a particular date. The suit was for conversion of property and the respondents had failed to prove their possession by leading evidence. Held also, that there was clear admission of the appellant 's father in his written statement that the land was left in the encroached area and that the appellant had not been aware of it at all. The courts below were right in holding that the respondent had knowledge of it and the burden of proof having been wrongly thrown on him, the suit had to fail.

The appellant was a crosscutter. It was alleged that the Secretary of the appellant had been suspended and asked him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on account of grave indiscipline and misconduct. The appellant replied that he had come to the mill at the relevant time for taking his wages for that week. The same day, the appellant informed the same day that in view of his denial, a departmental enquiry was held and he was also placed under suspension pending inquiry. The Industrial Tribunal found that something appeared to have happened on the afternoon of June 21, 1958 but there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened. It further held that the appellant could not be said to have taken disciplinary action against him for misconduct. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the employer could defend the action under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without giving any reason and therefore its action could not stand on a different footing as in the present case. The Tribunal had rightly held that there was nothing more to be said and that the industrial court could inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(b). The appellant failed to satisfy the tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication that the exercise of power in this case was bona fide and was not colourable. The fact that the enquiry was not held by the appellant and action was taken under r 18(c) did not make any difference. The industrial court had the right to inquire into whether there was a cause that might be sufficient or not and therefore having failed to justify its action must suffer the consequences.

The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for declaration that it was entitled to have a "exhibition rights" in the theatre. The trial court passed an order restraining the respondent from interfering with its right of exhibiting cinematograph films and the appellant was directed to hand over vacant possession of the theatre and to exhibit cinematograph films. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court failed. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that (1) the High court had no jurisdiction to record any finding on the issue of res judicata; (2) the trial judge erred in holding that the question whether a party is entitled to lead evidence or not was a matter which could be decided by the trial court and on which the opinion of witnesses was irrelevant, and (3) the consent decree did not operate as res judicata because a consent decree is merely the record of a contract between the parties to a suit. HELD : (1)(a) The High Court had no power to record an order of "court in the course of a suit" amounts to a "decision" within the meaning of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [445 B] (b) The question whether the party is enti tled to lead any evidence or to put questions in cross examination of the plaintiff 's witnesses cannot form the subject matter of an issue. [441 C] (c) The trial judge had rightly held that the High COurt had no jurisdic tion to record a finding on issue No. 11 in a revision application filed against an order refusing to uphold an objection to the question asked to a witness under examination. [442 E] (2)(a). The true nature of the order brought before the High Courts and the dimensions of the dispute covered thereby apparently got blurred and the High Curt proceeded to decide matters on which no decision was till then recorded by the Trial Court, and which could not be decided without the parties had opportunity to lead oral evidence thereon. [443 E] The true character of an order brought in appeal before the Supreme Court under section 115 Code of Criminal Procedure is derived from section 115 C.P.C. The High COrt has no jurisdiction on principles of resjudicata to go into that question or to decide it finally. [444 A B] In re: H.R.C., ; referred to. (b). The order passed by the High Court is set aside and the Trial court is directed to proceed and dispose of the suit.

The respondent was appointed as a pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was found unfit by an order dated 31st March, 1983. He was invalided from I.A.F.I.L. and was discharged on 30th August, 1985. The said term was extended from time to time subject to the suitability of the official concerned but not beyond that date unless there was a further extension. The respondent filed a Writ Petition in the High Court challenging his termination order contending that he was entitled to be reinstated in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period of his appointment beyond 30th of August,1985 or not unless there were a further exten sion. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ petition was liable to be dismissed. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the order of termination was an invalid one since it had been issued on the basis of Vigilance Report and no opportunity had been given to the respondent to show cause why such action should not be taken against him. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court has while setting aside the order dated 24th March, 1988 directed that the respondent was entitled for salary upto 30th September, 1985 unless there is a further Extension. [243D] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent had not urged before the High court that the Order of termination issued in his case was not in the nature of a contract and the subsequent orders extending his period of appointment till 30th October, 1985 were liable to he ignored and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to continue till he completed the age of 58 years. [244E] 1:3. The order passed on review was wholly unsustainable. [245F] 2.1 In the penultimate paragraph of the judgment dated 24.3.1988 it is stated that the High COurt had while setting out the Vigilance Report, considered the Vigilance report and no further extension of service. If the respondent were really aggrieved by the Judgment dated 24 3 1988 he should have preferred an appeal before this Court and that was not done.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses was not reliable, conflicting and improbable. HELD: (1) The discrepancies in the evidence were of a minor character and that they had been unduly magnified by the Sessions Judge. The discrepancies were in regard to which of them woke up first, where was the lantern and which of the neighbours came first to the scene on hearing their cries. The witnesses were not able to identify if they saw the accused making a gesture as if he was stabbing the deceased. The distance between the two places to the place of occurrence was 6 miles. The location of the injury was 6 cms below the arm pit on the left side. According to the prosecution, the victim received an incised wound in his hand and that the doctor who examined him found several abrasions and contusions on the person of the accused. The plea of the appellant that he had no deep motive to kill his wife and that his version was more probable than the version of the occurrence was not accepted by the High Court. [368 D E] (2) The discrepancy in the statement of the doctor was of a major nature and it could have been explained by the prosecution. It was obvious that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. [369 G] Sheo Swarup vs State of U.P., ; , applied. Sheo Swarup 's case, referred to. (3) The High court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. R. Fantle reported in (5) Salmon J. in Khem Karan & Ors. vs State, A.I.R. 1970 S.C. 1423, applied.

The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for two years under section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court dismissed his appeal against conviction and sentence. In the appeal before this Court it was contended that (i) the President of India could not be removed from his office unless and until he had been given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed removal; (ii) the provisions of section 6(1) (c) were not applicable to the case of a Judge who was not a member of the Higher Judicial Service; (iii) the High Court was in error in holding that the President could be removed only by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament in the manner provided in Article 124(4); and (iv) the power to punish a Judge under section 6 of the Act was very wide enough to include Judges of the High Courts as well as Judges of other High Courts. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The President is given the power of appointment and promotion of a judge of the highest Civil Court as well. [297G] 1.2 The President of the India could be treated as the competent authority to remove a Judge either of the, Supreme Court or of the high Courts. The President, therefore, being the authority competent to appoint and to remove him from his duties, must be deemed to have been the competent Authority to grant sanction for prosecution of a person who holds such an office. [298B] 1:3. The word "office" in section 6 (1) of Act is wide enough not to include judges of the higher judiciary but also for the other offences under clauses 4 and 5 of Article 124. [299D] 1 :4. The expression "office", in clause (c), has to be read as a part of the scheme of the Constitution, which includes the office of Chief Justice of a High Court. [300E F] 1I2. The words "office or office" in clause 2(a) have to be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of the competent authori ty under section 4 of the . [300F G] 1l3. In other words, if the holder of a public office during his tenure in office cannot be prosecuted without sanction under section six(1), it will follow that he will be immune from prosecution not only under section 161 but also under section 165 of the Indian Penal Code. [301B C] 1 4.

The appellant was a member of the Saha caste. Abhoy Pada Saha and Sudhir Kumar Mondal were members of a Saha caste, a Scheduled Caste. Abhait was a sub caste. The appellant challenged the election of Abhiman on various grounds including the ground that Abhoys had not belong to the sub caste specified in item 40 of the President 's Order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant did not belong either to the Scheduled Caste or to any Schedule Tribe and therefore, he was not a member belonging to the Schedule Caste specified in Item 40. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Abhaits were originally belonged to the Sunri caste but for a long time past they had formed themselves into a different caste which had no connection with the Suniti caste and therefore did not fall within the Sunti caste. HELD: (i) The order of the High Court is set aside and the election petition dismissed. [390 B] (ii)The appellant must be held to belong to a Scheduled Tribe specified in items 40, 41 and 42 for he said "these Sahas" within the meaning of Item 40 of that Schedule. It is legitimate to think that if the excluded Sahas were those Suniti by caste, both things are of the same kind; if one is a caste. the other must be a caste; it follows that when the item excluded Saha 's name is a Scheduled caste, the word "Care" in the expression "excluding Saha" in item 41 must, without more. also refer to a caste group within the bigger caste group of Sunri Caste. [391 C D] (iii) The appellant was not entitled to succeed on the ground of his being a member in the Saha ' caste specified by item 40.

The appellant was convicted under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the appellant had demanded a sum of Rs. 30,000 for the furniture and the motor garage in question from the respondent No. 1 and that the latter paid him Rs. 29,500 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs, 2,000 was paid to be paid to the appellant. The appellant pleaded that he had been in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence and that he was also to be a caretaker of his flat and as such could not pay the rent directly to the respondent. Held, that the word "relinquishment" used in section 19(1)(a) of Bombay Rents. Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, LVII of 1947, is not a term of art and was intended to convey or indicate an assignment of the tenancy and not a relinquishment of his tenancy by the tenant. The words "the relinquishment of tenancy of any premises" in section 18 are wide enough to include the transfer by a tenant of his interest which he has in the lessor. The word "distin quently" does not occur in the Transfer of Property Act but it is found in many of the Tenancy Acts in various provinces where there are Sec tions which deal with the relinquishment of their holdings by tenants in favour of the landlord by notice given to him in writing.

The appellant company was a partnership firm. It functions as a consulting organisation and a service industry. The workmen were members of the Tata Consultancy Engineers ' Association. They served a Charter of Demands in July, 1974 on the appellant and as their demands were not accepted they filed an application before the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication under section 10(1)(d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The claim of the Union was resisted by the appellant who maintained that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the union were accepted. The Tribunal held that the new scale of pay had been fixed in accordance with the recommendations of the Fourth Pay Commission and that there was no reason why the existing scheme of dearness allowance should be disturbed when a substantial increase was being made in the level of basic wage. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the Tribunal had not considered the range of permissible retrospectivity and that the financial capacity as the Tribunal observed was very much more than plain and plain that the increase in the dearness allowance and house rent allowance could be justified only if the demand of the company was accepted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The award was a composite document in which the several elements of increased wage scales, larger increments, longer span of 20 years for earning increments, dearness allowance at 10% of basic wages, besides several other benefits, have been integrated into a balanced arrangement in keeping with what the Tribunal has found to be the financial capaci ty of the appellant. [176F G] 2. The financial capacity, as the tribunal observed, constituted one of the principles which are required to be followed in fixing the wage structure. It is not necessary that the wage scales should be revised in every case. The basic idea underlying the award is to give a flat increase of Rs. 150/ to each workman in addition to the benefits conferred by the revised pay scales and other awarded reliefs. [177G H] 3. The Industrial Tribunal has given satisfactory reasons for adopting a different mode and it is not disposed of on merits. It has given cogent reasons for adopt a different method. [178A B] 4. The tribunal was wrong in giving a different scale to the appellant company. The order dated December 22, 1978 of the Tribunal is set aside and the Tribunal directed that the pay scales of different categories should be fixed with flat increase in each category. [179C D] 5. The additional financial capacity of the workmen would be more concerned with the immediate benefits according to them That was why the Industrial Tribu nal thought that an all round flat increase should be made in every flat cum industry cum industry. It did not give any ad hoc increase of salary, and therefore, it took a different view. [180F G; 181A] 6. The appellant company is directed to pay the additional dearness allowance to each of its employees in the category of Draftsmen and Rs. 100/ in the case of other categories. [181B] 7. The payment of dearness allowances to each employee should also be made with reference to the basic wage scales pertaining to different categories. The revised wage scale had necessarily to commence with figures Rs.150/ in that category. The revision of the wage scale was necessitated by a change in the basic pay structure. [182C] 8. The new scale had, therefore, to commence from December 22. 1978 and it would be necessary for the workmen to fitted into the revised scales of pay, it would obviously result in serious anomalous situations. While workmen raising industrial disputes for revision of wage scales are certainly minded about their future prospects in the matter of wages, they surely would be much concerned with immediate benefits which may be due to the immediate benefit according to their That was what the Industrial Tribunals had found in making the award dated December 20, 1978. [183E F] 9.

The respondent, an award made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/ per day and in pursuance thereof, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the award. This agreement was subsequently published in the Bihar Gazette as a part of the award, and in spite of the Award, the appellant paid its employees only As. /10/ per month and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The Tribunal held that section 2(vi) included wages fixed by an award in an industrial dispute between the employer and his employees and that the refusal of the employer to pay to them wages at the rate awarded, in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant to pay the respondents the said prescribed wages. The High Court affirmed this finding of the Tribunal. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The provisions of section 2 (vi) are applicable only to the wages fixed under the award but not to the workmen. [417 B] (ii) The terms in question need not be express and can be implied; but they must be terms which arise out of the contract of employment and since an award is made and it prescribes a new wage structure, in law the old contractual wage structure becomes inoperative and its place is taken by the wage structures prescribed by it. [420 C] (iii) The fact that on references made under section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, terms of employment have invariably been examined by industrial adjudication and wherever it appeared appropriate to make changes in them, they have been made in accordance with well recognised principles of fair play and justice to both the parties. Therefore, the basic assumption made by Mr. Setalvad that section was not applicable to the case because the wages prescribed by an Award could not be included within the definition prescribed by section 2 of the , before it was amended in 1958. [416 D E] (iv) The effect of construing the unamended definition of wages is that the old wage structure became inoperative and the place is take by the wages structure prescribed under the Award. In a sense, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between the parties because that, in truth, is the effect of industrial adjudication. [414 E F] (v) The amendment has merely clarified what, in our opinion, was included in the unamended section 2. The development of industrial law during the last decade bears testimony to the fact that, on references by the Industrial Tribunal, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages prescribe by the Award cannot be treated as wages under section 2.(vi) of Act before it is amended.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department of Pepsu. He was charged with having dishonestly removed certain medicines from a hospital which he had taken to his residence and misappropriated them. The trial court convicted him under section 465, Indian Penal Code for forging the thumb impression of Parma, and under section 409 of the Indian Penal code for criminal misappropriation of Rs. 51 shown as paid to him for his wages. On appeal by the State Government the High Court held that proof that the thumb impressions in the acquittance roll were that of the appellant was sufficient to establish an offence either under section 466 or section 409, and that there having been an acquittal of the accused by the trial Magistrate, the materials on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate court. The State appealed to this Court with certificate granted by the High Courts. It was contended for the appellant that the prosecution had failed to establish that the amount drawn by him did not reach the hands of Parama and that therefore no sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure could be taken against him. Held, that the conviction of the respondent was illegal as sanction under s. 197(I) of Code of criminal procedure was necessary for prosecuting a public servant under section409 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and the absence of such sanc tion was fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. The fact that the appellant had been acquitted by the Trial Court did not affect his conviction. The sanction under S. 197 (1) was required only in cases where the official character of the person giving the information was found to be irrelevant or extraneous. The mere fact that a public officer was involved in the very act complained of as amounting to a crime, would not make him liable for prosecution under section 196(1). Hori Ram Singh vs Emperor, A.I.R. 1948 Pat. 75, approved.

The appellant was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Travancore. It carried on the business of manufacturing and selling cotton, jute and other goods. The assessee company was assessed under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, to income tax for the assessment year 1950 51 with respect to its business profits made in the erstwhile State of Cochin. In the case of the appellant, it claimed that the business losses incurred outside Travancore State were not liable to be taxed as business profits and that the profits were exempt from tax under section 32(1) of the Indian income tax Act. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income Tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred in British India from its profits accruing and arising in that State. The Appellate Tribunal held that the Banking business of assessee being a business in British Indian, the assessee could not be taxed under section 7(1)(c) of Act 4 of 1922. On reference, the High Court held that it was not necessary to set out the reasons for allowing the appeal: Held, that the expression "business" in section 2(15) of Travancore Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1941, means business in India and not a business which is carried on by or on behalf of the asses see. The words " business " occurring in section 4(3) of that Act were used in the context of the proviso to section 24(1). Arunachalam Chettiar vs Commissioner of Income tax, Madras, ; , distinguished. Arunachalam Chetty vs Commissioner Of Income tax; , and Arunachalam Ayyar vs Commissioner o/Income tax, , referred to.

The appellant company was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company. It had branches in Bombay, Delhi and Via. The General Manager of the Company at Calcutta raised a dispute regarding their retirement age. The Tribunal held that the age of retirement should be 58 but the Company could not retire from service before he bad completed 60 years of age. On appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant company that the Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to fix the age at 60 and that the Company may in its discretion and with the express or implied consent of the employee concerned continue an employee after he attains that age. Held, that the Tribunal had rightly held that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court in Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs Workmen, ; , that the question whether it should be fixed at 58 or 60 was a matter of policy. The fact that the appellant Company wrote to the Bombay Chamber of Commerce to ascertain from its member concerns as regards the age was wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend. It is not necessary for the Tribunal to add in this connection, that what had been done by itself was correct and they must speak for the period both before and more particularly after the previous finding had been recorded in the matter. Dunzolop Rubber Company Ltd., Via, vs Workmen ; , referred to. The award of the Tribunal is set aside and the award made by it is restored. DunZlop rubber Co. vs Workmen. [1960] 1 S.C.R. 869, distinguished.

The first respondent company was incorporated in 1961 and its incorporation in the year 1961. The Board of Directors of the Company passed a resolution on May 19, 1965 to sell certain shares of the company to the first respondent. On June 4, 1965 the first appellant issued an order under section 237(b) of the appointing 4 persons as inspectors for investigating the affairs of the respondent company and also appointed one of them as Inspectors for investigation into the affairs. The first respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said order on the ground that the Board had no jurisdiction to pass the impugned order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the power conferred on the Chairman by section 237 (b) was administrative and not judicial. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the powers conferred on him by section 236(b), were exercised only to make what was implicit in section 10E(5) read with section 642(1) clear and that the distribution of the work of the Board being merely a matter of procedure, the order of the Chairman transferring the functions under section 9(b)(i) to himself did not amount to sub delegation of the power of the board. HELD : (i) The power conferred by section 235(b). is administrative in character and not administrative. [334 B] (ii) The powers are exercised for ascertaining facts and circumstances which indicate that the business of the first company was being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other persons or persons. It is only when such a power is conferred by statute that it can be validly exercised by the Chairman of the Boards. [330 C] (iii) The Board has no power to delegate its function under section 236 to itself and therefore the order passed by the first appel lant is invalid. [328 D] (iv) The order made by the Board is not invalid because it was made by a Chairman of a Board. It was not challenged in any court.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . In appeal by special leave it was contended that the presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, because dacoity as such is not challenged before this Court. HELD : The conviction was correct. If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. There is then no question of presumption. The evidence strengthens the other evidence already against him. It is legitimate therefore to raise the presumption in this case that the persons with whom the goods were found were the dacoits themselves. [724 D E] In the present case, the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market and they have been presumed to be involved in the dacoity itself. The time gap is too short for original offenders to have disposed of the property to these appellants or to have left the goods in their custody till such time as the original offenders could take them away. [700 E F] In this case, there was no other evidence in the present ease which points to the complicity of the 14 appellants in the crime of dacoity and therefore as they cannot be suspected to be dacoits themselves, the only presumption to be drawn is one of receivers of stolen property or as receivers of property which was stolen in a dacoity.

The petitioners, who were carrying on business in poisons, challenged the constitutional validity of Section 5 of the (12 of 1919) (which was enacted as a Central enactment) and section 5 of that Act. The petitioners contended that the impugned provisions violated Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution inasmuch as they had not placed any matter before the Advisory Board constituted under the Act, which was competent to make Rules in exercise of this power under Section 3 of the Act. Dismissing the writ petition, HELD: 1. The provisions of neither section 2 nor 5 are hit by any consti tutional limitation. [222D] 2.1 No comprehensive definition can be given to the word poison. Under this term it is intended to control over the traffic in poison. It states that the State Government may by rule regulate the import, possession and sale of poisons. Some substances which are used for purposes mentioned therein can certainly be declared as poison. That is what the Government have done in this case. [223E] 2:2 The provisions contained in Section 2(3) of Act, impliedly sets out certain guidelines when the State can notify a substance as poison and that the same is left to each State Government to determine what substance they would include as poison for the purpose of the . [222F G] 2 :3. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance as an poison for sale and the sale of the specified poison. It is in exercise o this power Rule 13 was amended by substituting the old rule by following Rule 12. [224H;225A B] 2 .4. The Notification and its applica tion to any areas would depend upon the necessity for declaring the substance, as poison on the particular facts and situation prevailing in that area and the need to regu lute the possession and sell of the same. It was not all poisonous substances that were brought within the regula tions under the . The notification did not contain any such guidelines when it was amended. [225B C] 2 5. The provision of neither Section 2 nor the impugned notification are hit either by any con tentional limitation or any infirmity. The writ petition accordingly fails and is dismissed.

The appellant firm was carrying on business of importing yarn and other goods. The assessee firm had a business relations with a firm known as M/s. Bhojji Mulchand, one of its partners in the firm. In the books of account of the firm it was shown that the amounts due to the Bombay firm were not loans advanced by the firm but by the Bombay Firm and the Income tax Officer treated them as bad debts and taxed them under section 10(2)(xi) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer but on further appeal the Tribunal held that the debt did not arise in the course of the assessee 's business as chemists and druggists nor in the case of any other business of the appellant. In reference to the High Court under section 66(2) of Act, the Tribunal referred to the Full Bench the question whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the debt of Rs. 2,68,385/ was not one incurred in the ordinary course of business of assessee '. The High Court answered the reference against the appellant firm. On appeal by special leave: Held (i) that before the question may be answered, it is necessary to call for a supplementary statement of case from the Tribunal and to consider whether the finding reached by the tribunal are findings of fact and those findings are supported by proper consideration of the material before it. The Tribunal after catalogueing the arguments advanced at the bar, has come to certain abrupt conclusions but all the tame it cannot be denied that the findings reached by it are findings based on no evidence or that they are supported either by proper discussion of the materials before it or by application under section 11(2). The conclusion reached by Tribunal is not supported by any proper discussion. (ii)The conclusions reached by both the Tribunal as well as the High Courts were binding on this Court. The question whether the debt or any part thereof was in respect of loans made in the special course of its money lending business of a company, depends upon the facts of each case and the circumstances in which it was created. In order to decide whether a debt or an amount is one incurred by a person carrying on a banking or money lending, the Court has to consider the evidence and the material produced before it and to see whether the material placed before it is sufficient to support the finding. The material before the Tribunal is such that it cannot reasonably be denied its jurisdiction to decide the question raised in the appeal. (iii)The conclusion reached on the basis of the findings of the Tribunal are not supported either from proper discussion or by proper understanding of the relevant evidence. It is also true that the tribunal after catalyogueing, the arguments advance at the Bar, has came to certain ob jections but all these cannot be controverted and it must be held that this finding reached on a consideration of all the circumstances and those conclusions are supported not by proper reasoning. The conclusion arrived at by the Tribunal was binding on the High court.

The facts of the case are highly material. The interim orders have a direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. [567F] 3. In view of the provisions contained in section 11 A of the land Acquisition Act to which we have already referred, it is beyond dispute that the fact of stay orders were highly material and the petitioners had failed to make out a case for relief. The non disclosure was very material in their determination only when the respondents appeared in response to the notice and filed their counter affidavit. [568F G] 4. The appellant company was incorporated in 1953 with the object of securing basic pay on January 1, 1962. The first group consisted of workmen who were drawing basic pay at a particular stage in the time scale of pay applicable to them under the Sastry award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal decision dated April 1, 1965. In the second group there were workmen who entered service of the bank before 31st January, 1959 and were paid dearness allowance on the basis that they would be fitted in the new scales of pay provided by the Sastry Award as modified from time to time. The appellant company claimed that the workmen would be entitled to increments as provided under the Desai award as they were not satisfied with the fixation of their pay by the appellant bank under para 5.356 of the Sastry awards as modified and were not entitled to increment in the revised scale. The Labour Appellate Tribu nal held that the adjustment basic pay was to be fixed on January 31, 1959, and that the adjusted basic pay in the old scale would draw basic pay from January 1. 1962 and thereafter they would he fitted in new scales with effect from January l, 1959. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant company that the adjusting basic pay had to be taken as on January l. 1959 and not on January I, 1959; that the adjustments were made in accordance with cl. (ii) of para 292 of the Desai Award as amended by the award as amended and that they were only entitled to those benefits which were given to workmen or the maximum in the existing scale of the pay provided for by the said Sastry Award. HELD: The adjustment basic salary in cl. 5.3 of the award was not to exceed what point to point adjustment would give an employee on January Ist, 1962 and therefore when cl. 2(a) speaks of adjusted basic wage it must refer to the same date as in cl.(iv) which provides for actual calculations starts with the words "subject to rules (i) to (iii)" and therefore the actual calculation made under el. (iv) must be subject to clauses (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv). [903 D E] The adjustment in cl, 5. 3(a)(1) has to be calculated as on 1st January 1959.

The appellants, who were the owners of a residential building in Calcutta, applied to the State Government for four acres of land which was not available. The State Government refused to grant the said four acres on the ground that it had no title to the land and that the land was not used for the main purpose of the Zoo. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the decision of the Cabinet. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the decision to lease out the land to the Taj Group of Hotels was taken on February 12, 1981. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the policy of the Government to grant four acres to the five star hotels was contrary to the policy and that if the land is to be allotted to the hotels, separate provision would have to be made for them. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The policy of granting four acres is not to earn revenue from sale of resin but to promote the setting up of industries within the State. It is only in cases where the Government has made available to the court all documents in connection with the proposal for lending over a piece of the State Govern ment land to respondent No. This is how the High Courts deal with aspect of the case in its judgment. [260B C] 1.2 The policy decision taken by the Cabinet on February, 1981 was merely to enter into negotiations with the I.T.D.C. and the Taj group of Hotels in regard to leasing out a portion of the land for the construction of a Five Star Hotel. The Government was quite alive to the need for expanse ment of the zoo or the facilities provided in the Begumbari land for its use. [261F G] 1:3. The policy that is being followed by the hotel group to start with, was not known to the law such as acquisition or requisition. It was not forgotten that if it was assumed that the Government had the power to transfer the land, the Government did not have the power of dealing with the land in any manner that they liked. The object of the state in such a case is not merely to earn income from sale and the facilities for the use of the site were being provided in this regard. [262C D] 1 :4. The purpose of granting the four acres was to start a Five star hotel which, according to the Government was a very important need to the city of Calcutta. It would result in an unhealthy atmosphere for the animals and the zoological Garden increasing as a result of planting numerous trees all around the proposed hotel and the removal of the burial ground and burning ground for rubbish. The proposed hotel is a Garden Hotel and there is perhaps every chance of the ecology and environment improving as a consequence of planting several trees all over the city. [263D E] 1 5.1 It was also not forgotten in the State Policy that the hotel was a Garden hotel and there was perhaps every possibility of the environment improving. The proposal to grant 4 acres of Begumbar land to a Hotel was, therefore, justified in proceeding on the basis that the Land which was undoubt edly Government land, to start its Five Star hotel, which according to it betrays unawareness with the method of calculation to be adopted in similar cases. This was not done by the State in the face of the assurance given by the Chief Minister that facilities would be provided for the Zoor and the playgrounds. The reasons for the delay were also not explained. [264F G; 265A B] 2.2 In the instant case, the land which had been Government land was given to the Zoological Park upon the terms set out in the two letters. The letter of the Director of the Board of Revenue dated June 29, 1981 addressed to the Secretary to the Home Department stated that the Zurich hotel was not a public place for accommodating the existing facilities.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, had two houses in Calcutta and the relevant date of valuation was 31st March 1957. The assessee had directed the company to debit his account to the extent of Rs.50,000. On 1.1.1957, the assessee made a gift of Rs 25,000 from his account. The gift was effected by debiting the assessee 's personal account in the books of account in respect of the firm whose accounts were said to be credited or debited. In the case of banking companies or other firms and companies who have overdraft facilities, even if the sums are not in credit of the donor and are not with such companies or firms gifts might be possible by adjustment of the book entries. The Income Tax Officer held that there was no valid gift of the principal amounts as there was a valid gift and therefore the assessee did not make any valid gift. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In reference, the High Court held that the gifts were valid and the interest paid in respect thereof could not be included in the net wealth of the assessee. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave against the decision of the High court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in answering the question in the manner it did. [130D] 2. In case there was not sufficient cash balance from out of which the amount gifted could be physically given to the donee, more entries in the accounts of the account in his books of accounts would not constitute delivery of possession over the gifted property to the donor. [131E F] 3. The fact that the assessee had made a valid gifts of Rs 50,000 to his son and to his wife respectively did not indicate that he was entitled to retain the possession and enjoyment of the property to tho entire exclusion of the donee or, to the entire exclusion from the exclusion of donor or, as the case may be. [132F G] 4. The entries in books of a bank by credit and debit, do not constitute valid gift but only make it clear that the transaction was genuine and there was nothing in them which could be said to have been credited in the account of the minor donees. [133G H] 5. In view of the fact that there is no registered deed and as there is a book entries in respect to the firm, the question whether there was valid gift or trust in respect thereto does not arise. [134A B] 6. The question whether the assessee has made a proper gift or a trust in favour of his son or relatives is a matter which must be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case. [135C D] 7. In order to find out whether there is valid gift, the Court has to consider the effect of the entries in a particular book by credit or debit, and it is not necessary that the entries should be made contemporaneo nately or with such alterations as may be necessary for the purpose of ascertaining the real intention of the parties. [136E F; 137A] 8.

The Orissa Superior Judicial Service ( postings, etc.) Rules 1963 were framed by the State Government under section 3 of the Orissa Superior judicial Services (Seniority, Pay and Allowances) Act, 1964. The rules provided that the High Court shall not ordinarily interfere with the administrative officers ' work unless they are given an opportunity to show cause against them. The High Court was requested to send back judicial officers working in administrative posts as district judges or as addl. district Judges as the case may be, after they had held those posts for three years or more. The State Government accepted the request and appointed the High Courts as District Judges. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the power to appoint the secretaries to the government is exclusively vested in the Chief Justice. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) Under article 235(b) of the Constitution the Governor is only concerned with the appointment, promotion and posting to the cadre of district judges but not with the transfer of district Judges already appointed or promoted and posted to the Cadre which power is vested in it by article 235 as the control given to the High court over the District Courts under that Article includes control over the officers who preside over those courts. [161 F G] (2) The power to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of articles 233 and 235 is exclusively with the High Commissioner. It is true that in the course of the judgment this Court observed that the rule laid down in that decision was of no assistance in determining the question as to whether the High 'Court has power to fill up some of the posts in the secretariat by transfer judicial officers under its control. But, in view of the decisions of this Court in State of West Bengal vs Nripendra Nath Bagchi, ; and State of Assam vs Ranga Mahammad, ; , it was not correct to say that the rules laid down therein were ultra vires.

The appellant company was incorporated in the State of Gujarat on December 14, 1969. Its workmen were not entitled to sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness following at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of illness for which the employees claimed maternity leave. The workmen also felt aggrieved by the award of the Industrial Tribunal, Gujarat, dated September 24, 1975, in the dispute between them. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award on the ground that the benefit of sick leave was not available to workmen in Baroda with effect from December 14. 1969 and they were quite adequate, the Tribunal committed an error of law in granting the additional benefits mentioned above. The High Court held that the workmen are entitled to 7 days ' sick leave with wages on full pay on the grounds of sickness. It also held that there was no practice of giving any such sick leave in the industries in Baroda or in the States of Gujarat, and that the appellant had not been able to show that the awards in question were illegal or unjust. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that as the benefits granted by the Tribunal are not similar to those admissible under the Act, they are quite adequate and the Tribunal commit ted an error in granting them. HELD: (i) The scheme of the benefits admissible under section 49 of the , cannot be said to cover the work men 's demand for sick leave to the extent allowed by the Industrial Tribunals. Section 61 of the Act does not provide for any leave to a workman on the basis of sickness, and even that amount is not admissible for the second time in the present case. [84 E] (ii) The Tribunal was justified in granting additional benefits to the workmen under the scheme. [85 G] (iii) The award in the instant case was made effective from December, 14,1969. It has not been disputed before this Court that till then it was the practice in the glass industries to grant sick leave without regard to sick leave. [86 D E] Technological Institute of Textiles vs Its Workmen and others ; , followed.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the , and was served with a notice dated August 6, 1955, on him. He challenged his detention by means of an application before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the grounds were vague and did not contain any particulars as to which of the grounds could be furnished in public interest. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of detention was made without any real application of mind by the detaining authority, that the State Government had no power to make a representation against the detention under article 22(5) and that the failure to furnish particulars did not vitiate the order. Held: (i) The right to be furnished grounds of detention as soon as may be; and (ii)the right to have an opportunity to make representation is a fundamental right. The right of the detenue to be afforded the earliest opportunity of making a representation is not a mere formality. The obligation to furnish details and the duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest are vested in the detaining authori ty, not in any other. The requirement that particulars and the duties to consider must be furnished must be clearly stated in the order itself. The power to detain a person under section 7 of the Act as soon after may be, and not later than two months from the date of detention cannot be said to have been exercised without any basis. The failure to do so is an infringement of the constitutional right of making an effective representation against his detention. The mere fact that the detaining au thority did not at all consider the grounds furnished in the grounds, would not make him a person who had no opportunity to meet the grounds. The order of the State Govern ment must be taken to have made out a case for consideration on a consideration of the circumstances of each case as well as the ambit of the non disclosure of facts made by the Under Secretary to the Government of Bombay by means Of his affidavit in answer to para 15(g) of his petition.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre. He was charged with having committed acts of gross misconduct. The Chief of the Army Staff, after going through the proceedings of the Court of Inquiry, considered that the conduct of the appellant was most unbecoming of an officer. The Central Government directed removal from service of the respondent. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal on the ground that r. 14 of the Defence Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the , and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (i) the provisions of the Rules were ultra vires as they had been enacted by Parliament under Entry 41 of List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution; (ii) the words "subject to the Act" occurring in section 19 make section 19 subject to the provisions Of the Act and such rules, the Central Government may dismiss or remove from service any person subject to this Act. HELD : (1) The Army Rules, 1955, are ultra vires. They do not confer any power on the Central Govern ment to remove an officer without being tried by a court martial. [449 B] (2) The words " subject to" in section19 make section19 subject to section 45 and the Central government has thus no power to remove a person from the service in derogation of the provisions contained in section 45. But the power under section 19 is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words 'subject to this provision ' it speaks of removal of a person ' from the Service. Section 45 provides that on conviction by court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. [448 C D] (3) The word "subject" used in section 20 makes section 19, subject to which the Central Govt. has no power. It follows that there may be a valid rule where under subject to other provisions of this Act, the central Government may remove a persons from the serv ice. Under section 19(2)(a) specifically gives power to make a rule providing for the removal from the ' service of persons subject to that Act. [450 C D]. (4) The expression "subject with the provisions" occurring therein in section 18 makes it clear that there should be rules and subject to such provisions as are applicable to the Central, Government may provide for.

The appellant was assessed to octroi duty under the C.P. & Berar Panchayat Act, 1946. The respondent filed a petition in the High Court challenging the levy of octroi duty on the ground that it was not imported into the limits of the Panchayat for consumption, use or sale and that the appellant had failed to fix the octroi limits in accordance with law. The High Court held that the tax was not validly levied by the Panchayat as it had failed before the Standing Committee to fix octroi limits. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Rule 5 of the Taxes and Fees Rules framed under section 3(b) of the Act provides for appeals against levy or imposition of any tax or fee. The appellant has not shown that the Panchayat Samiti or the Standing committee had found sufficient facts to enable it to deal with the question. Therefore, the High court was right in holding that the levy was illegal and ultra vires. [222 B C] (ii) Rule 3(a) does not require the Panchayat to fix its octroi limits for consumption use or Sale. The expression "taxes on pilgrims" is used in a wide sense and includes all taxes levied and collected by a panchayat. The word "tax" has been defined in section 2(11) of C. P. & T. Act, 1947, as meaning the levy or collection of any duty or fee or tax. Therefore the fixing of the octroi limit with the approval of the Collector is an essential condition precedent to the levy and the rules are not confined to octroi duties only. [223 E G] (iii) Rule 4(b), which authorises the levy is r. 22, does not contemplate that the procedure prescribed in rr. 3 and 4 should be followed before the octroi duty can start being levied. The fixing of octroi limits with the sanction of the Government is an important condition precedent for the levy. [225 B] (iv) Rule 6(b)(i) does require the Panchayats to notify to the public not only the proposal about the tax selected by it for levy, but also the rules relating to that tax which must mean the action taken under the Act and the Rules. The Standing Committee inspected the premises of the Company but in its order they have given very scanty facts and did not say whether the tea is crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. [226 C D] (v) Rule 7(b). of the Rules requires that the notice following the decision of a Panchayat to levy any tax, or fee, should be published by affixing a copy thereof in the office of the panchayat. If so read, it would mean that before the Octroi duty can commence being levied, r. 21 must be complied with.

The appellants were the Andheri Marol Kurla Bus Service who was accused No. 1 and its Manager, H. M. Khan who was also appellant No. 2. The evidence showed that the conciliation proceedings had been concluded for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952, further proceedings for conciliation were illegal and therefore the appellants were convicted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1). Held, that the proceedings did not end when the report under section 12(6) was made by the Conciliation Officer but when that report was received by the appropriate Government it was to bring about settlement between the parties. The conciliation proceedings could be prolonged only when the reports were received by a Government and no settlement was arrived at. Workers of the Industry Colliery, Dhanbad vs Management of the industry Colliery, (1878) L.R. 7 I.A. 65, referred to. Held, further, that as 14 days had expired before March 18, 1952 the dismissal could not be said to be one within the words " pendency of conciliation proceedings before a conciliation officer ". The provisions Of section 12 of the , were applicable only to all the conciliation proceeding under the Act and not to all proceedings in respect of which an industrial dispute is referred. Workers ' Union vs The Industrial Tribunal, Bombay, ; , referred to and applied. The Bengal Immunity Co. Ltd. vs Management, of the Industries Colliery, and The State of Bihar vs Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga, (1952) L I.L.R., Lah. 861, approved.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he had been arrested in connection with a criminal case registered against him. The grounds stated that there was indiscriminate firing by the petitioner and his associates, who were there to be killed. The detention order was served on or about 11th January, 1986. The petitioner challenged the order of detention before the High Court which dismissed the petition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the order was passed on one incident relating to exchange of fire between two rival groups and that there were criminal cases against the petitioner. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The principles applicable in these types of preventive detention cases have been discussed in the decisions of Suraj Pal Sahu vs State of Maharasthra & Ors., W.P.(Crl.) No. 3 96/86 with SLP (Crl) No. Crl A. 353/86 and Ramesh Yadav vs District Magistrate Etah and others, ; , referred to. 2.1 The grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the order as contemplated by the Act and the materials on record. The principle applicable in those types of cases has been discussed and applied in the decision of Surajpal Sahu vs The State of Maharashtra & Ors. ; and Ramesh Singh vs District Magis trate Burdwan & Anr., ; , followed. 2:2 In the instant case, there were allegations of criminal cases which had been filed against the detenu. There was no indication that this factor or the question that the said detenu might be released or that there Was such a possibility of his release, was taken into consideration by the detaining authority properly and seriously before the service of the detention order. If there were cogent materials for thinking that the detenu might have been released then these should have been made apparent. [910C D] 2.3 The grounds of detention were not on proper consideration. It may be mentioned that in the affidavit of the District Magistrate, though there are indications that transfer of the detenu from one prison to another was considered but the need to serve the detention Order while he was in custody was not properly considered by the Detaining Authority in the light of the relevant factors. At least the records of the case do not indicate that. If that is the position, then however infirmityable the antecedents of a person might have be taken into considera tion by the detenu properly and effectively before the Service of the Order. [1010G H; 1011A] 2:4 In the present case, when the actual order of deten tion was served upon the detenu, the detenu was in jail. There is no indication in the petition that this fact or the questions that the alleged detenu might he released or was likely to be enlarged on bail. The service of detention order therefore, is not on valid consideration. [1110C] 2 :5 In the affidavit on behalf of the detaining author it has been stated that the petitioner was in Jail. There are allegations of mala fide against him and his activities were prejudicial to public order. In these circumstances, the continued detention of the petitioner under the Act is not justified. It is well settled in this constitutional framework that the power of directing preventive detention given to the appropriate authorities must be exercised in exceptional cases as contemplated under the various provisions of the different statutes dealing with preventive detention and should be used with great deal of circumspection. There must be awareness of the facts necessitating preventive custody of a detenu for social defence.

The appellant, a manufacturer of gold, was manufacturing gold. The respondents were manufacturers of gold and were dealers in gold. In the assessment proceedings for the year 1965 66 the Income Tax Officer held that the appellant had not been able to prove that the gold was smuggled into India. He also found that the respondents had not produced any evidence to show that the goods were smuggled into the country. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Income tax Officer. In further appeal, the Tribunal reversed the decision of the Appellate Authority holding that the licence fee paid by the appellant for the gold in question was not sufficient guidance to enable the Administrator to grant or renew a license to a dealer. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The objective, the policy and scheme of the Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the , afford more than sufficient guidance for granting relief against the same he will be guided by the policy of the Central Government. [955D] 2.1 In the instant case, the object and purpose of the enactment and the scheme affords sufficient guidance in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. The main object is to provide for providing, in the economic and financial interests of the community, for the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and business in gold ornaments and articles of gold. [951F G] 2:2 In the present case, there was no express rule prescribing the conditions or circumstances under which the permission can be granted or refused. The object is not to provide any blanket or absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on money lending, banking or any other business in the same premises in which he carries on business as a dealer but he is prevented only from carrying out such business as would be permissible. [953F G; 954A] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise Poona, ; and Ramanlal Purshottamamdas Chokshi vs Union of India & Ors., , referred to. 2.3 The objective is the policy, the Policy and the Scheme giving sufficient guidance and the necessity for ensuring prevention of circumstances which may be considered. [952B] Harkchand Ratan Chand Banthi vs Assistant Collector of Customs, ; , followed.

The appellants were the owners of agricultural lands situated in Eragudi village, Musiri Taluk, Tiruchirappalli District. The said lands were alienated from time to time and as a result of the last alienation, the appellants became entitled to them. The respondents filed a suit against the appellants claiming a declaration that they had acquired title by adverse possession. The trial Court found that the grant was a personal inam and that it was not a grant in favour of the religious endowment within the meaning of section 2(2) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951. On appeal, the lower appellate court held that the lands were granted in Inam to the respondents and they were not holding the same as managers of the trust. The High Court also held that it could not be said that the appellants had acquired a title by hostile possession prior to 1st January 1929. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether the facts proved in the present case did not show that the alienees had been removed from management of the temple de facto, has not been discussed by the High Court. It is open to doubt whether the said decision could lead to the inference that if a part of the property was transferred by the manager on the basis that it belonged to him and not to the religious endowments, the transfer is void ab initio, with the result that the possession of the transferee is adverse to the temple from the very beginning. [693 D E] (ii) The fact that the alienation made by the appellants in favour the respondents was for a valuable consideration does not affect the application of article 134 B of the Limitation Act. It only applies to cases where it is shown that the immovable property was comprised in the endowment and that the transfer was for valuable consideration. [651 C] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding that the title of the respondents had not been lost by adverse posses sion before the suit was filed. [641 D] (iv) The contention that the transfers with which we are concerned in the instant case fall outside the purview of article 135 B is without substance. It does not mean that the intention of the legislature must be gathered from the language used and the words used therein must be understood in their ordinary sense. In construing a statute, it is necessary to bear in mind the object of the Act. The words used are "transfer effected by a previous manager on behalf of the public". If the property is transferred by a manager not as manager but as an individual, he has no longer any interest in the property and his right to challenge the transfer would be lost if his predecessor who made the transfer lives for more than 12 years after effecting the transfer.

The appellant, a licensee of the respondent firm, filed a suit against the respondent for a declaration that the cinema licence granted to him by the District Magistrate in favour of Ved Gupta was invalid and illegal. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the renewal of the licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, namely, Shri Ved Gupta who had been declared to be the sole licensee in respect of the Apsara Theatre by the proceedings of his predecessor in interest. The High Court allowed the appeal filed by the respondent and quashed the order passed by the trial court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the District Magis trate directing the suspension of the cinema shows in the Theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. [557B] 2. The impugned order is one obviously passed by a District Magistrate, in exercise of his function of administering the provision of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. The implied power to take all steps necessary to ensure the due observance of the terms of the statute, the rules and the conditions of the license as otherwise the competent authority under the Act would have to be a helpless spectator when cinematograph films are publicly exhibited by persons other than licensees. [586C D] 3. The licensing authority has no jurisdiction to suspend the licence. It is now well settled that the power to control the exhibition of cinematography by grant of licence and the power of administering and enforce the provisions of the , is conferred only by section 6 F of the . The impugned Order passed by District Magistrate directing suspension of cinema shows therein in the theatre cannot be held to have been violative of principles of natural justice. [596G H] 4. The power to suspend a licence is conferred on the licensing authority and it can issue such an order as may be necessary or expedient for regulating the grant of licences and the rules made thereunder, clearly includes the power under section 6F of the Rules. The Order is one necessarily passed by an appellate court in exercise Of its function of administration of the law. [606G] 5. The writ petitioners were some of the partners of the firm who wanted to run the Theatre without a licence in contravention of the provisions contained in the Act, and the statutory authority had no jurisdiction under the . [616A B] 6.

The appellants were displaced persons and on 30 8 1952 the respondent issued a notice to them under section 12 of the , stating that they had systematically committed breaches of various terms on which the properties bad been leased to them. The appellants challenged the validity of the notice, contending that section 12 was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under section 10 of the Act and that the notice was ultra rites. Held, that the respondent was acting within his authority in issuing the notice under section 13 of the . The provisions of the section clearly indicate that the Custodian has the power and had always the power to cancel leases created not merely by the evacuees but also by himself. But he con tended that the powers conferred on him by section 12 could be exercised only so as to override a bar imposed by any law but not the contract under which the lease was held, and this result flows according to him from the language of the non obstante clause which is limited to anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs Arabinda Bose, , applied. The operative portion of section 12 which confers power on the Custodian to cancel a lease or vary the terms thereof is unqualified and absolute and that power cannot be abridged by reference to the provision that it could be made "notwithstanding anything containedin any other Law for the lime being in existence". The operative part of the Section which confers powers on the custodian to cancel contracts created not only by the evacuee and not by himself, but also on him.

The father of the respondent, who was a minor, executed a deed of sale in favour of his grand father, maternal grand father of his minor. The Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, by his order dated 10th August, 1972 determined the ceiling area for Raghubir Singh and his son Surendrapal Singh as well as the surplus land measuring 4 Bighas and 6 Biswas. He also held that the land in possession of the father was ancestral. The respondent filed an appeal before the Revenue Appellate Authority, which allowed the same and remanded the case to the Sub Divisional officer, Hanumantha, for fresh determination of the calling area for the Raghubir Singh. The order of the Sub Divi sion Officer was set aside by the Board of Revenue on March 6, 1973 and remanded to the sub Divisional officer to determine the land afresh in accordance with law. The Board held that there was no provision for separate units in Chapter III B of the Act of 1955. In pursuance of the direction of the Board, the Sub divisional Officer passed an order dated 5th May, 1976 holding that the father and son constituted two separate units and each one of them was entitled to get 62 Bighas, 16 Biswas and 6 Biswa only and the surplus area measuring 4 bighas and 6ani had been resumed.
