The appellant filed a revision application before the Board which allowed it and remanded it to the Subordinate officer for fresh deter mination of the call area for enquiry. The matter was taken up by the Sub Divisional Officer to hold that there is no provision in Chapter 111 B of Act of 1956 for separate unit in Chapter IIB of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955. The writ petitions filed by the appellant were dismissed by the High Court. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 221 of the Punjab Tenancy Act is not subject to the other provisions of the Land Revenue Act and it is clear from the language of section 221 of that Act that the Board has general powers of superintendence and control over all revenue courts. It is open to the Board to exercise its powers of supervision on all its subordinate courts in order to regulate the functioning of the subordinate courts so as to keep them within their respective spheres of jurisdiction. If the subordinate court disregards any specific provision of law and does something illegal it is open for the Board or Revenue to interfere and set the matter right. A similar question arose before the Rajasthan High Court in Kana and others vs Board ofRevenue, Rajasthan, ILR where the High Courts had to construe the power of the Boards to set aside the order of Sub Divisional Officers provided it comes to the conclusion that interest of justice requires exercise of such powers. [726B C] 2. Section 222 of the Code of Civil Procedure is similar to section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915 and there is nothing illegal in it.

The first respondent, a journalist, was engaged in the production or publication of the said law reports. The first respondent filed an application before the Central Government under section 12 of the , praying for the benefits conferred upon him by the Act. The Central Government rejected the claim of the first respondent and held that the law reports published by it were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act and that the demand made by the Deputy Labour Commissioner to comply with the order made by him on the basis of the recommendations of the Palekar Tribunal was unsustainable. The High Court accepted the plea of the Ist respondent and declared that the Law reports published were not newspaper as defined in the Act, and that they were not the newspapers within section 2 (b) and therefore the orders made by them were invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the two courts reports published in the law report were not presses but only newspaper reports which could be said to contain news so as to become newspaper. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law reports which are being published by the Ist Respondent are newspapers and the employees employed by the first Respondent in their production or publishing of the law Reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by the Central Govern ment on the based on the recommendations made by Paleakar Award. [778C] 2. The expression "newspaper" is not defined in section 2 of the . The law report which are to be published by a newspaper and also comments on some of the recent decisions. Though the publication of these items by itself may not occupy a substantial part of a law report to make it a newspaper, the publication does not cease to be a newspaper within the definition of "new 'paper ' in the . [780E F] 3. The word "new" is used in the sense of "an journalist". It is not understood in the context of any particular case whether newspaper or newspaper is a newspaper. The term "newly closed" has been defined by section 2 to mean any person employed to do any work in, or in relation to, any newspaper establishment. [783G] 4. The definition of the expression "Newspaper ' is usually applied (except so far as concerns the important class of trade newspapers) to publications devoted mainly to recording current events and `periodicals ' to magazines, reviews, and journals which in so faras they are concerned with current events at all, are concerned to comment rather than to report; but newspapers merge into advertising sheets, periodicals into books and pamphlets and both into one another. [784C D] 5. The publication of items by themselves may not be a substantial portion of a newspaper report to making it a paper, but the publication is sufficient to make a law reports a newspaper which may after some time cease to he a newspaper or become a book of reference.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises since about 2nd February, 1965. On or about 9th February, 1966 a fresh document was executed and it was alleged that the appellant continued by virtue of that agreement. The appellant filed an application for eviction against the respondent on the ground that he was a sub tenant of a business concern. The trial Judge passed a decree in ejectment petition filed by the respondent and ordered the appellant to vacate the premises before 31st March, 1988. The High Court refused to interfere with the finding of the trial court that the respondent was a licensee and not a subtenant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the appellant was not a tenant as such or licensee; (2) the Court of Small Causes Bombay had no jurisdiction to deal with the eviction petition in this case; and (3) the court of Small Cause Court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finding of High Court that the Respondent was a tenant is a licence and not licence. good deal of submission was made before this Court that if it was a lease and not license then this point could be taken in aid of the submission that the court had to jurisdiction and there was no estoppel. [21D] 2. The expression "B.C."" was used in section 15A on the 1st day of February, 1973. The word "B C" is used in the context of the Act. In order to get the advantage of section 15 A of the Bombay Rent Act, the occupant must be in occupation of the premises as a licensee as defined in section 5(4A) on the Ist of February 1973. But if he was not merely a licensee under a subsisting agreement on the first day of January, 1973 then he did not get the benefit of the amended provision of the said Act. [22E F] 3. The Court of Appeal in England again in Cobb vs Lane, ; , held that where it cannot be said that there was a clear error apparent on the face of the record, the error if any has to be discovered by long process of reasoning and the High Court should not exercise jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution over such decision. [23F G] 4. In view of the fact that the parties had been carrying on business for some time, it was not possible to determine whether the appellant proved himself to be a sub lessee or not. The question whether the respondent is a tenant or licensee depends upon the construction of the document and the facts and circumstances of this case. [24F G; 25A] 5. In the instant case, the appellant had been in occupation for some period prior to the termination of his tenancy. It was a licence which he could have obtained under the Rent Act. The respondent had not proved that he had gone to occupy the suit property any time before that date and the dispute started only from the date of the agreement. In fact, the rent light bill stood in the name of the respondent showing that there were no desire to create any lease by the document mentioned therein and the appellant regarded him as a mere licensee. The tenancy was not for a sub lease. [25G H; 26A] 6. The background of the facts of this ease is clear from the entire document negate the contention of the appel lant that it was merely a licence. The document created an interest in the property, it is a license and not as a lease. good dealing of submission made before the trial Court was a license. [26B] 7.

The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute between him and the State of Rajasthan related to a time before merger of former Dhol Purshat in 1949. The case of the respondent was that in 1947 certain commodities including chuni with which appeal No. 887 was concerned, were taken away from the former princely State into the United State of Rajaswa and thereafter the former State of Dholpur came to be included in the United States of Rajasthan through the Matsya Union. The respondent claimed that he had been granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni from the latter State on the basis of an agreement dated January 26, 1950, which was entered into by him with the Government of India and which was accepted by the Government. The suits were resisted by the State on various grounds but the High Court held that the liability of the State to refund the amount collected in advance for no export was not fasten on the respondent as it emerged from the agreement dated February 26,1950, and therefore the State was bound by the obligation of the latter to refund it. The State appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the liability to refund could only be determined by the Ruler of the erstwhile prince State of Jaipur, and (2) the agreement had been recognised by the new sovereign and therefore article VI of the Covenant could not operate to confer any right on the company as against the new State. HELD : (i) The new sovereign throughout this process of integration from 1948 onwards was in its entirety an act of State and that article VI did not apply to it. [179 E] (ii) The agreement dated 26th January 1950, was a mere recognition of the rights of the subjects and the new Government had no right to recognise them as sovereigns and that the new state assumed liabilities of the old laws and under the circumstances the suit was main tainable against the Part B State of Jodhpur. [180 G] (iii) The appellant could not be allowed to raise a contention in this Court that the agreement was recognised by it. It is true that in the present case the new Ruler had been recognition by the New State throughout this period and under section 3 of the covenant, all the assets and liabilities of tho Covenanting States were to be the assets of the new States must have intended to respect all the rights flowing from laws so continued and assume all liabilities arising from the existence of those laws. [181 G] Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. vs The State of Saurashtra, ; , followed.

The appellants were dealers in commercial crops. They sold their produce to a third party at the market rate and paid the price of the commodity to them. The appellants contended that they were not entitled to any deduction under section 14 of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, as amended by the Amending Act of 1955, because, they had only two fundamental rights: (1) that they did not achieve the object for which they were enacted but were also prohibited from holding their business as property; and (2) that the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder constituted reasonable restrictions on a citizen 's right to do business. Held, that the appellants were not liable to pay any tax under the Madras Sales Tax Act, 1939, as it was not a trade allowance within the meaning of section 14 Of the Act. The provisions of sections 4 and 5 of the impugned Act read with the bye laws framed thereunder showed that the Act did not impose reasonable restrictions upon the appellants ' fundamental right to carry on business and therefore they were valid. The Act did provide for the better regulation of buying and selling of commercial crops in the Presidency of Madras and for that purpose to establish markets and make rules for their proper administration. The object of the provisions was to eliminate, as far as possible, the middlemen and to give reasonable facilities for the growers of commercial crop to secure best prices for their commodities. The fact that the market committee did not name the allowance or allowances taking them out of the provi sions under section 15 of the , did not make any difference in the matter. The impugned provisions of Act, as they stood before the amendment of 1955 by the amending Act of 1956, showed that there was no restriction on a person 's rights to do trade or business and that the restrictions imposed were reasonable. The imposition of the tax was therefore valid.

The appellants were convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their convictions and sentences. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that (1) the conviction should be maintained but the sentence in each case should be reduced to transportation for life; (2) the appellants were not guilty and so should be acquitted of the offence under section 34 of the Penal Code; and (3) the High Court erred in holding that the death sentences on the three appellants were illegal. HELD : The conviction must be maintained. The sentence of imprisonment for a term of ten years will suffice. That leaves the question of sentence in the case of Bhilia and Tukia. It is not enough as in the present case, to have direct proof of prior concert or proof of circumstances which necessarily lead to that inference, or, as the case may be, to determine the conclusion on the facts in another. All that is necessary is either to have a direct proof or proof, of circumstances, which necessarily leads to that conclusion, or ,, as it prefer to put it in the time honoured way, "the incriminating facts must be incompatible with the innocence of the accused and incapable of explanation on any other reasonable hypothesis". The case of the appellants was not one of mere preponderance of accusation but one of a strong character. [1091 H; 1092 A B] In the present ease, the circumstances disclosed do not warrant an inference of common intention in the instant case. There is no evidence to show that there were any prior meeting. It was also not proved that the appellants had been guilty and convicted of the murder. The conviction of the appellant must be set aside.

The petitioner was appointed as a Section Officer under the Ministry of Works and Housing in the Central Public Works Department on 22.10.1947. He was compulsorily retired by an order dated 3.8.1976 made under Rule 56(j) of Fundamental Rules. The vires of Rule 56 (j) was challenged before this Court by the petitioner who was a Section officer in the Ministry. This Court held that the impugned order was contrary to the judgment delivered by this Court and did not require to be re examined. It was further held that Rule 56 was meant to cover only those who were in a post on a regular basis i.e. in a regular manner, i. e., in a class or Class II service or post. The petitioner had crossed the age of 50 years but had not attained the age Of 55 years by the date of the order. This court held that it was meant for the benefit of all Government servants and sub clause (i) carves out a class of Government servants into a category and makes a special provision. It further held in Tahiliani 's case that sub clause(ii) did not apply to the facts of this case as the petitioner had not attain the age at the time of retirement. The Court also observed that sub cl.(i) was not attracted to the case because the petitioner was holding an officiating appointment in Class I or Class 11 service or a post, on substantive basis. On this conclusion the writ petition was allowed and the order of compulsory retirement made against each of the petitioners was set aside. Allowing the Special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The ratio of the decision in Tahilani ' 's Case is not correct and sub cl (i). of Rule56(j)(1) applies to Government servants in Class l or Class I service or posts on substantive, temporary or offi cial basis. [637C] 2. Sub clause (ii) of Rule 55(j), which applies to government servants in class I or class II service and post on substantive. temporary oroffi ciating basis, is meant to covers only those Government servants who are in Class 1 or Class III service or Post, on officiating basis. Instances are abundant where officers are promoted to Class I and Class II Service or posts in such a service or office as covered by sub clause 2. The possibility of such incumbent being sent back to the substantive post is not at all relevant in the matter of exercising powers of compulsory retire ment.

The respondents, who were husband and wife of the deceased, filed a suit in the Subordinate Court for recovery of Rs. 50,000 on the ground that the deceased had died intestate on 12th January 1961. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation and that the respondents did not commit any breach of contract. On appeal by the Corporation, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the Subordinate Judge and held that there is a concluded contract of insurance between the respondent and the Life Insurance Corporation of India. In this appeal by certificate it was contended for the appellants that the proposal was not accepted and as such there was a concluded insurance contract between them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in appreciating the facts and evidence in this case. [359E] 2. The plea that the Divisional Manager was the only competent authority to accept had not been categorically taken in the written statement filed on behalf of the Corporation. It is true that normally the expression "underwrite" is used in Marine insurance but the expression used in Chapter III of the Financial Powers of the Standing Order in this ease specifically used the expression 'underwriting and revivals ' of policies in case of Life Insurance Corpora tion and stated that it was the Divisional manager who was competent to underwrite policy for Rs 50, 000 and above. The general rule is that the contract of Insurance will be concluded only when the party to whom an offer has been made accepts it unconditionally and communicates his acceptance to the person making the offer. Whether the final acceptance is that of the assured or insurers, however, depends simply on the way in which negotiations for an insurance have progressed. Having regard to the clear position in law about acceptance of insurance proposal and the evidence on record in this Case, it is not possible to accept the High court 's criticism with the averment in the plaint that there were no concluded contracts and non acceptance of the proposal by the Divisional Office was not sufficient averment that theDivisional Manager wasthe only competent authori ty to accept. [360F G] 3. The contention that there Was no concluded agreement and non receipt of the proposals was not correct. The Corporation had not filed any evidence of any order prohibiting other officers one step below in rank, in this behalf.

The plaintiffs applied for an interim injunction restraining the Bank of India from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s. V.V.S.R. Export, Moscow, the second defendant. The trial court granted an interim order restraining encashment of letters of credit pending disposal of the suit. In appeal the High Court set aside that order and remanded the case to the trial court for trial. On remand, the trial Court passed a decree in favour. The plaintiffs applied to the High COurt for a certificate under article 133(1)(a) and (b) of the Constitution. The High Court held that an order granting interim injunction was a final order as far as this Court is concerned and that it was not a final decision on the rights of parties in dispute in a suit or proceeding; and that the expression "final order" in article 133 (1)(c) must be read ejusdem generis with the words "final orders". In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High CO. Court had no jurisdiction to grant the certificate. [701 D] The expression " final order" is an interlocutory order and is not a "final" order within the meaning of article 133. It has been held by this Court that an interim judgment even if it decides an issue or issues without finally determining the rights and liabilities of the parties is not final. In the present case, the High court was concerned merely with an order passed by the High Co. Court in a petition for winding up of a company as to the maintainability of a claim for recovery of income tax dues. [700 E F] The question whether an interim relief should be granted or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If the rights are in dispute, in the suit or proceedings, then the order is interlocutory. [601 G H] In the instant case, there was no final decision as to whether a particular claim was personal or not. The expression 'final order ' has been used in contradistinction to what is known as "interlocutory order". It has also been held that the finality of that order is not to be judged by co relating it with the controversy in the complaint, viz., when then the appellant had committed the offence charged against him therein. [ 700 G H; 700 A] The trial Court decided the issue against the appellant and the order was confirmed in appeal by the appellate court. In an appeal under article 132 and a revision application before the High Curt which did not finally dispose of a suit, it was held that it would be a final disposal of a dispute in the civil proceeding from which appeal had arisen, as the trial Judge had committed no error in holding that the right to parties to the property was personal to the appellant.

The appellant company was manufacturing processed fabric and manufac turing the processed fabric. The excise authorities treated the value of the processed fabrics as the assessable value of processed fabric, and assessed the same to duty under section 3(1) of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The Assistant Collector confirmed the demand of duty on the basis that the value was the assessablevalue of the grey cloth in the hands of the processor plus the value thereof. On appeal by the appellant company, the Tribunal held that the assessable valuation of the goods should be the value for the purpose of the excise duty and not the value which would be taken to be the price at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market. Dismissing the appeal by Revenue, this Court, HELD: 1. The assessable value is the value as determined by the Assistant Collector of Central Excise under section 4(1). [346C] 2. The valuation of goods owned by one person are manufactured by another and the information is required relating to the price of the processing profit and the manufacturing expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It is necessary to include the processor 's profits who gets the fabrics processed, because those would be post manufacturing profits. [346D] 3. The factory gate as if the processed cloth was sold by the processor. In order to explain the position it is made clear that the market value of goods should not be the valuation under the Act and the rules made thereunder. [347E] 4. If the trader, who entrusts cotton or man made fabric to the processor for processing on job work basis, would give a declaration to the fabric as to what would be the prices at which they would be sold in the open market, that would be taking by the Excise authorities as the valuation of such goods and not any further subsequent profit. It was not necessary to add the trader 's profit to the concept of the price for the grey fabrics or fabric plus the values of the job work done plus manufacturing profit and manufacturing expenses.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On April 1, 1975 he was confirmed with effect from March 14, 1975. The appellant challenged his absorption on a lower post and filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that by reason of section 14(4) of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1961 the appellant was entitled to continue in service of the Panchayat on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the Panchayats Samiti until they were absorbed in Government service or retire in such manner as may be prescribed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment of the appellant to the post of a Head clerk in 1963, long before June 13, 1973, was not recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13 1973 when the Amending Act came into force. There is no substance in this contention. Even assuming for the purposes of argument that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant had the right, to appoint him to the posts of Head Clerk or on April 1. [738C D] 2. The fact that the appellant is promoted as Head Clerk in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed lawfully to the Post of a clerk and that he is appointed lawfully does not alter his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after July 13, 1972 when the amending Act came in force. [ 738E] 3. The order of the Government of Haryana notified the absorption of the appel lant as a Clerk though as stated earlier he was working as a head clerk in the Loharam Panchayat Samiti. He is therefore entitled to be absorbed in government service as a clerks in any event. But, as a result of the deletion of section 33 of the Act by the Amending act of 1973, the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. The Government of Punjab notified the absorbing of the appellants as a junior clerk on April l, 1975 or the other fact that they were appointed as Head Clerks on April1, 1975 cannot improve his position.

The appellant was the Mahant of a Math, and installed a deity acclaimed by the name of "Gokarneshwar Mahadeo" installed in the Math. The property was purchased by the Mahant from his predecessor Shivshankar Yati. The income tax authorities assessed the appellant to income tax for the years 1951 52 and 1952 53 on the basis that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity and that the appellant was in possession thereof as Mahant and Sarbarakar. The High Court allowed the appeal of the appellant holding that the Amauli properties had been purchased by Shivshanker Yati from the personal and separate funds inherited by him from his predecessors in interest and that he was entitled to possess, enjoy and acquire personal property. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that where a nucleus of dedicated property exists, the acquisition of additional property should be attributed to the application of the nuclean Yati; that the income tax from the properties belonging to the math and the deity left any appreciable surplus after meeting the expenditure on account of bhog, arpan, deepdan, daily and annual puja and the other obligations specified in the waqf deed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The fund from which the Amaulty properties were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shivsarayan Yati and did not form part of the properties of the Math, Sauna. [663G] 2. In assessment proceedings under the U. P. Agriculture Income Tax Act 1948, the Amauri properties constitute the personal properties of Mahant Shiva Shankar Yati, and do not form parts of the property of the math Sauna nor of the deity. Small parcels of these properties were transferred by Mahant Shiv Shedutha to the appellant 's predecessor in interest. The properties were purchased by him for Rs. 40,000 from his successor Shivswar Ji Maharaj. He was granted a succession certificate by the District Judge, Varanasi, in respect of the two fixed deposits made by him in the Bank of Bengal. Mahant Shiv shankar Yat, who executed a will in 1956 bequeathing certain properties to the deity with the intent that arrangements for bhog would be met from them. The appellant was granted succession certificate under section 6 of the U P. Agricultural Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1964. Mahant Shiva Shanker Yati died on November 12, 1924 and his heirs were brought on record as legal representatives. The question whether the fund was the personal or separate funds left behind by his predecessor ininterest was not raised before the High Court. [665B C] 3. The appeal is dismissed.

The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. The Custodian of Evacuee Property, Punjab cancelled the allotment of certain quasi permanent allottees of evacuee property in the same district on the ground that they had been wrongly fitted in the village released upon cancellation of allotment of land in their favour by reason of cancellation of the allotment in their names. The appellants filed a revision application before the Custodian General but the same was rejected on the grounds that r. 102 of the Rules framed under section 12(1) of the Act empowered the Central Government to acquire evacuee property for rehabilitation of displaced persons by publishing in the official gazette a notification to that effect, and that the notification issued thereunder was invalid as it had been made after the commencement of the , and the notification was therefore invalid. The High Court dismissed the revision application on the view that r, 102 did not apply to the case because the cancellation was a result of misapprehension of the actual facts and that they were not entitled to allotment of suburban land at all. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (i) the Custodian had no power under section 10(1), to cancel the allotment; (ii) the notification dated March 24, 1955 issued by the Central Govern ment under section 13(1)(a) of Act 1 of 1954 was invalid because the order of cancellation was erroneous and (iii) the cancellation of allotments was a colourable exercise of powers. HELD : (1) The Custodian had not been in possession at the critical time they would have had the right to obtain a permanent transfer in their name. [337 B] (a) The provisions of section 19(1 ) of the Punjab Act do not apply because the power of the Custodian under section 19 is confined only to properties which are entrusted to them for management and not with respect to any other property. Therefore, even if no managing officer or managing corporation was appointed with respect of that property no one else could exercise the power. [333 C] (b) The fact that subsequent to the issue of the notification under section 11(1). of the .the Act, the property would cease to be evacuee property and the said powers of the custodian would be in conflict with those conferred by section 19 of the 1954 Act on a managing officer and managing corporation. [332 G] (c) The contention that there was no entrustment in fact of this property or this class of properties to a managing agent or managing Corporation could not be accepted.

The State Public Service Commission, in its report dated May 5, 1985, recommended the recruitment of the two Scheduled Caste candidates and five Backward Class candidates to the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Career) ( Gravity). The selection committee after considering the merits of the candidates found that in the process of re spondents ' recruitment examination, the entire recruitment examination would stand vitiated. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Service Com mission cancelling the entire recruit ment examination and directed the State Public Services Commission to re hold the examination afresh. Allowing the appeals by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written examination and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the written exami nation, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina tion. [126B] 1.2 In the instant case, when no defect had been pointed out by the High Court, the State Government could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the basis of the written test and select those who on the date of the examination and in terms of the recruit ment rules fresh selections shall be made. [127C D] 2.1 The situation could have be appropriately met if four years had been appropriately re cired by setting down the interview examination. There was no reason for cancelling of the selection test. On the facts alleged, there could have also been proper met by set aside the appointment and asking the High Courts to dismiss the writ petitions. [128D] 2:2 When no defects were pointed out, the Court could have directed that a fresh examination be held for re holding of the examina tions and asking a fresh exami nation of all the written examinations shall stand dissolved. The State Public service Commission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the exercise of the power to cancel the entire selection examina bits would not have been lost and the public cause would not be suffered.

The appellant brought a suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala, that this institution had two branches one at Landeke in Moga and the other at Nanga Kheri. The suit was decreed by the trial court but the High Court reversed it holding that after the death of Som Dass, Shiam Dass, as his Chela "inherited the sum total of the rights which earlier vested in Som Dass and when a controversy is raised about such rights, then the appellant was bound to bring on record the legal representatives of the deceased within the time prescribed by law. The High Court further held that after taking evidence, the appellant could not be said to have any knowledge about the date of death of the widow. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The suit against the person upon whom the interest had devolved was sought to be continued against Shiam Das as de facto mahant of the Dera after the demise of Som Das. [488B] 1.2 In the instant case, the suit was filed on the basis that the appellant as the lawfully appointed mahant was entitled to manage the properties attached to it. The appellant had no right to recover possession of the property of theDera. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest of the representative, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22, Rule 10 and not rule 3 or 4, whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason. [489C D] 1:3. The word 'interest ' which is mentioned in this rule means interest in the property i.e., the subject matter of the suit and the interest is the interest in property i,e.,, the subject mater of the Suit and the interests is the interests of the person who was the party to the suit. It was, however, contended on behalf of the respondent that there is no devolution of interest in tho subject matter in the suit on death of a previous mahant by virtue of law or custom that there would be devolution of inter est in the subject of the claim of the appellant. When the suit is filed by oragainst a person, in a represen tative capacity and the appeal is sought to he continued against the persons acquiring the interest with the leave of the Court, it cannot be continued under Order 22 rule 10, because the head of the mutt or manager of the temple resigns his office or is removed from office. [490C E] 2.1 In the present case, there was no certainty as to the person whom would become the mahant if he was elected to be the Mahant of the dera after his death. The fact that it was after Som Dass died that Shiamdas was elected as mahant. The appeal could not therefore be continued by the respondent.

The Andhra Pradesh State and Karnataka had framed the Andhra Pradesh Civil Service (Classification, Control & Appeal) Rules, 1979. The validity of these rules was challenged by some of the petitioners who were working as Junior Engineers in the Andhra State. They contended that the age of retirement was increased from 55 to 58 years with effect from October 29, 1979 after an elaborate and scientific inquiry by a committee constituted under Rule 2 of the Andhra Civil Service Rules, and nothing had happened since then to justify reduction of the age. The Government of Andhra Pradesh rejected their claim for premature retirement on the ground that they were not competent to reduce their age. It was contended that there was no basis at all for reducing the age as it was arbitrary and unconnected with the object which it sought to achieve. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The power of the Governor under Article 309 is a legislative power and the Legislature has the power to make provision for removing the difficulty arising in the exercise of such power. [655E] 1.2 The Government had exercised its power arbitrarily without having regard to factors which are relevant on the fixation of the retirement age at 58. It is not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case. The recommendation of the Second Central Pay Commission that the retirement should be raised from 55 and that the said recommendation was accepted by the State Government and consequently, the age was raised to 58 with effect form the date of retirement. [557F G] 1:3. The fact that the decision to reduce the age is taken by the Government cannot justify the conclusion that it is arbitrary because it is unscientific in the sense that it was not backed by due investigation or by compilation of relevant data on the subject. If reduction of retirement age from 58 to 55 is to be regarded as arbitrary on the grounds that it overlooks the advance made in longevity, fixation of retirement at 58 is also not likely to sustain the charge of arbitrariness. [60G H] 1 :4. The question whether the exercise by the Governor of Andhra pradesh was arbitrary or irrational and unconnected to the object of the Act has to be kept out of consideration in so far as the question of the power of compulsory retirement is concerned. [61C D] 2.1 It is well settled that the power conferred on the Governor by Article 309 can be exercised only for good reasons and not for any other purpose. The power to retire a Government employee, not being a workman and not belonging to Last Grade Service, shall retire from service on the afternoon of the last day of the month in which he attains the are of 55 years. [62E F] 2:2 It is difficult to appreciate how the exercise undertaken by the High Court of power can be challenged as lacking in authority. The recommendations made by the Second Pay Commission were not accepted by Government initially because it felt that raising the age at 55 was a fair and reasonable basis. The report of the Commission has therefore to be treated as a valid exercise of legislative power.

The Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973 was enacted to provide for the levy of purchase tax on goods other than those specified in Schedule B. Section 9(1) provides that where a dealer liable to pay tax under this Act, fails to make payment of tax at the first stage of sale under section 17 or section 18, he shall pay the tax payable by him in respect of the tax due from him in accordance with the provisions of section 9. The appellants who were dealers in raw materials in the State of Haryana entered into agreements with certain other dealers for the purchase of raw materials and sold them to dealers who in turn exported those goods out of India. On these facts, the Sales Tax Officer issued a notice u/s 9(2) of the Act to the appellants on the ground that they were liable to tax under section 9(i)(b). The appellants challenged the validity of the said notices before the High Court and contended that since the sales effected by them fell within one of the three exempted categories set out in section 9 (1) of Act, the same was not taxable. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that: (i) Section 9 (i)(a) does not provide for levy of tax on the sale proceeds of goods on which purchase tax is leviable under section 8 or section 9, and (ii) the expression "disposes of" used in clause (b) is inclusive. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The words "dispose of" in clause(a)(ii) of sub section (1), are wide enough to include cases where raw materials were purchased and exported and the word 'export ' was defined in section 2(c) as meaning "the taking out of the goods from the State to any place outside it". The words 'disposes the manufactured goods to a place outside the State in any manner otherwise than by way of sale in the course of inter state trade or commerce" are wide and include cases of despatches by a dealer of the manufacturedgoods otherwise than under section 5(3). [362B C] 2.1 The expression "dealers" is defined in Section 2(p) as including persons who were not specified in schedule B, except milk, from any source in the state and uses them in the said State in the manufacture of any other goods and either disposed of the manufac tured goods to the dealer or used them in his own way. [362C D] 2:2 The expression 'disposal of" is wide enough and includes within the definition of "turnover". The word 'turnover ' has been defined in s.2(c), as meaning the taking out from the goods by a person who purchases them from the market, to a places outside the state in any way otherwise than for by way off sale in tho course of Inter State trade or business. [363D E] 2 :3 The definition also excludes from its purview "disposals" other than "in the course ' of inter State trade and commerce". [362E] 3.1 In the instant case, the sales were effected by the assessees fall within one or more exempted categories. There can be no doubt that a tax is levied under the Act on the goods in question when they are sold by a registered dealer for the purpose of export outside the territory of India within the meaning of sub s.(1) and sub section 2 of section 5 of the Central Sales Tax, 1956. [361H; 362A] 3:2. The language of section 8(1)(a)(i) is wide and includes cases where goods are disposed of only by way o sale in inter Statetrade or in the inter State outside the territories of India, within the ambit of sub sec tion (1). [363B C].

The appellant firm was registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The goods were sent to the consignee for delivery at Bombay for the sum of Rs. 68,493. The consignee sent a letter dated September 27, 1954, to the appellant stating that he had purchased castor oil which they then sold for the amount of Rs,. 6,47,509. The appellant 's contention was that the goods remained their property till the goods were brought on board and so the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. Held, that the words " a person " in section 10(b) are wide enough to cover everyroute between the seller and the buyer. The words " the seller " in the latter part of the section mean the time when the goods cross the customs barrier. If therefore in the present case the goods went out of the territorial waters of India, the sale would not pass immediately before the ship goes beyond the territorial limits of India. The intention of the parties that the property in the goods would not passed till after the ship had passed beyond the territory of India was clear from the fact that the appellant 'had no knowledge of the intention and the fact remained that the seller intended that the good sold to him at some point of time before shipment, that is, after they had crossed the customs frontier. The word "the buyer" in section 8(b), as used in section 2(a) of that Act means the person who has given such certificate under section 8 (b).

The respondent divorced the appellant from her husband 's family. She was married to the appellant as a second wife, way back in 1956 and a few years later. The first wife filed a suit for maintenance against the appellant under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 alleging that she had transferred the suit premises to the appel lant and also the shares of the Co operative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. The trial court held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for her child. On appeal, the Sessions Judge enhanced the monthly maintenance from Rs.300/ to Rs.400/ . In revision, the High Court set aside the order of the Sessions judge and restored that of the trial court restored the order passed by the trial Court. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant 's case was a new statutory right created as a projection of public policy by the Code of 1973 which could not have been in the contemplation of the parties when in 1962 they entered into a contract to adjust their then mutual rights. [78 C] (2) The expression "wife" is used in the widest sense and includes a woman who has been divorced by or has obtained a divorce from her. [79 E] (3) The husband ' s claim absolution from this obligation under section 127(4) of the Code, because of the compulsive conclusion that the wife was not living separately for a day, even in that city where 40% of the population are reported to live on pavements, unless she was ready to sell her body and give up her soul. The whole scheme of section 127 (3)(b) is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the particu larly justice, specificated in article 38, fulfilment of which is fundamental to the governance of the country. [80 F G] (4) The legal sanctity of the payment is certified by the fulfilment of social obligation not by a ritual exercise rooted in custom. No construction which leads to frustration of statutory project can secure validation if the court is to pay true homage to the Constitution.

The appellant bid for the auction of a rice mill in an auction held on 27.3.88 and was declared to be the highest bidder. The Collector, after considering the representation made by the appellant, cancelled the order of the Collector. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the cancellation of the order. The High Court allowed the petition holding that black listing of the appellant was not necessary for giving any prior notice before black listing. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the State Government that there was no requirement specifically of giving any notice as no prior notice had been given to the appellant and that there is no requirement in the rule of giving prior notice. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The black listing order issued under the Collector 's order dated 25th March 1988 is not a mandatory provision of law. It has to be realised that black listed any person in respect of business ventures had civil consequence for the future business of the person concerned in any event. Even if the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order.[868D E] 1.2 The last portion of the Order in so far as it directs black listing to the appel lant is set aside. So far as the cancellation is concerned, that is not affected. This order will however not prevent the State Govt. or the appropriate authorities from taking any future steps for supervening public good. [868F G] 2.1 In the instant case, the last portion has been given by the rules framed under the Act to the Collector of the district after considering all the representations made against the proposal of black listing the appellant. The order dated 27th March, 1988 is set at naught. So it is quite clear that the black listed person S/o Late Gorakh Nath Village repura, P.S. Puksha, District Samastipur had civil consequences for the past business of his person concerned. Even assuming that the rules did not express any so, the respondent is right in law to pass any order in accordance with law indicating the reasons therefor. [8868F H] 2:2 The order passed by the Collector is set quashed and it is directed that the appellant be placed in the black list in respect to future contracts under the collector.

The appellant was the tenant of certain co owners. The respondent landlord filed a petition under section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, for fixation of fair rent in respect of the premises leased to him under two lease deeds dated 22 9 1947 and 3 10 1947. The first lease deed provided that the lessee was entitled to seek fixation of the fair rent at Rs. 150 per month. The second lease deed also provided that if the lessee did not pay the rent for three months, he would be liable to eviction from the leased premises. The Rent Controller held that the buildings on the land leased under two leases were conveyed to the appellant and that the appellant was entitled only to seek fix of fair rents in respect thereof. On appeal, the appellate authority confirmed the order of the Rent Controller. In further revision, the High Court held that since the subject matter of the lease was only a vacant site, the Rent Control Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for fixation or fixation of rent in view of the provisions of section 64 C of the Act and that therefore, the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the Rent Act was not maintainable. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that since he was only an intermediary, the rent could not be determined without jurisdiction, although it would have to be decided by the Rent Tribunal as a collateral issue in deciding certain applications before them. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question whether the denial of the landlord 's title by the tenant is bona fide or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [562D] 1.2 In order to decide whether the refusal of a landlord ' s title by a tenant is bonafide, the Court has to consider the nature and scope of the jurisdiction conferred on the Controller under the Act. It will be anomalous to hold that where an owner of property seeks to evict his tenant under section 10(2)(vii) but the Rent controller refuses to pass the order for eviction though satisfied about his title because the tenant had acted bona fide, it would be open to the owner to seek eviction by having his title adjudicated upon in a civil court but that the owner cannot have a similar right in the matter of recovery of rent which is basically a relief for which he has to approach a civil Court. [561E F] 1:3. The jurisdiction of the Controller, under section 11(4) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Conversion) Act 1948, is a statutory jurisdiction which is vested in the Rent control ler by the terms of the . It will not be open for the High Courts to entertain a collateral attack on the validity of binding nature or correctness of the order passed by the Court of Small Causes and to consider and determine afresh the issue as to whether the tenant has title adjudicated on the question. [560F G] 1 :4. The decision of the Additional Settlement Officer that the suit land was sold to the appellants and that they were entitled to recover the rent from the tenants, is not final on the issue that opens up his jurisdiction and cannot preclude an owner from contending in a Civil Court, that he should not be asked to pay rent for his own property to some one else. [559G H] 1 5. The question of title to the property is one on which his very jurisdiction depends. In order that a tenant may have to establish his contention on the basis of the evidence adduced by him, it will have to pass a decree in favour of the landlords on the strength of the same evidence. It would not be right to contend that the order in the earlier proceedings is to be treated as an order that is null and void or merely one that is valid until set aside, the answer has to turn on the true nature and effect of the decision in the first set of proceedings. [558C D] 1 6.

The Mysore State Civil Service Integra tion Rules, 1960 provide for filing objections to the preliminary list. The petitioner was given ample opportunity to object to the final list. He filed objections to a final list on an analogy with the second opportunity which was granted to him. The High Court held that the combined final gradation list dated April 6, 1962, so far as category 6 is concerned, was ultra vires and illegal and directed the re spondents to get opportuni ty of puting forward their objections before final list was prepared. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Central Government that the petitioner had ample opportunity of being heard and that he should have been given a reasonable opportunity to make representation with regard to these two points. HELD: (i) The combined final list dated 4th April 1962, is ultra vires. [830 B] Shankariah 's case, ; , followed. (ii)The petitioner respondent was not entitled to an opportunity to be heard against the final lists. [828 C] (iii)The High Court was right in holding that the conclu sioner had ample opportunities to make a representation with regards the two points urged by him and the Supreme Court had also to give a full and fair opportuni ties to the parties affected to make their representations; and the Central Govern ment has also to furnish a full, and fair opportunity to the respondents affected to makes their representations. [829 E] (iv)The second opportunity given to the petitioner was not adequate to enable him to make his representation with respect to these points. The Central Government had been unable to make out, in any manner, that those points were considered before finalisation. What was meant was that the publication gave the list finality. In fact what was meant by the second opportu nity which is afforded to a person to be punished after arriving at a decision on the facts of a departmental trial and proposal to inflict a particular punishment upon him, was quite inap propriate. [827 G H] (v)The Central Government has been given ample opportunities of being made parties by the petitioner.

The petitioners, a partnership firm carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of cut and polished diamonds, filed writ petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution in this Court challenging the validity of sub para (10) of Para 218 of the Import & Export Policy 1978 79 and also for a direction to the authorities to grant Export House Certificates to the petitioners under the Import Policy 197879. The petitioners contended that sub para(10) was intended to take in terms which were banned altogether as well as items which were prohibited for import by the holder of an Additional Licence, and that the word "banned" was intended only to take into account those items which are excluded under the Export Policy, 1978 79 but also from importing items excluded under Appendices 3 and 5 Part A of the said Policy. The respondents contended that the petitioners had failed to achieve the objective of granting the Additional Licences and the import policy and that there was no similarity between them and other persons who were granted Additional licences on the basis of their exports made during the period 1977 78 in accordance with the Import and Export Policy 1988 91, and the Export Houses who would be granted Additional Licences on or after April 1, 1988, on the ground that they had failed in the export of "other products" during the year 1977 78. The writ petitions were contested by the respondents contending that sub Para (10), para 218 of para 218 was intended for taking in terms of Import & Exports Policy 1978 80 and that under the said policy the basis for grant of Additional Licences was the f.o.b. value of exports, and not the Export House which was to be given on the strength of the order dated April 18, 1985. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners who were holders of Additional licences under the Imports & Exports Control Policy 1978 1979 79 have been granted an Additional Licences whereunder it is permissible to import items as per para 215 of the Export and Import Policy 1985 91 on the view that the petitioner 's claim for additional licence cannot be said to be persons similarly circumstanced. Under the Import Trade Policy 1978, there were two requirements for grant or renewal of Additional Licence: one was the condition that the value of the imports made by the Import House for the purpose of exporting goods is to be excluded from the fringed benefits of items of raw materials, components and consumables covered by Appendice (in Appendicating) Order 1978 79.

The appellant is a division of McDowell & Co. Ltd., which manufactures and sells fusel oil/styrene Monomer falling under Tariff Item No. 68 of the First Schedule to the Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944. The appellant was manufacturing and selling fusel oils/sties falling under tariff item No.68 of the first schedule to the Act. The goods were delivered from the factory in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer, there fore, the value had to be included in the assessable value. The Assistant Collector of Central Excise held that at the time of removal the goods were received from the appellant 's factory in packing condition and that the containers was not returnable to by the buyers, there being no packing material, the cost of packing could be included as part of the assessable price. The order of the Assistant Collector was confirmed by the Appellate Tribunal. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) since the Act provides for only one exception to this measure, namely, non inclusion of the cost in the value of goods when the packing is supplied by a customer to a manufacturer on its own cost, the price of the drums in which it is packed is not includible in the assess able value of the goods; (ii) since at the relevant time the goods are delivered from factory in pack condition and, therefore, the containers are not returnable upon by the seller to the buyer to the buyers; (iii) since there was no sale of packing which was liable to be excluded under clause 4(4)(d)(i), it was not necessary that the goods should be delivered in packed conditions and that in any event the cost incurred by the manufacturer on the packing was to be added to the price except where the packing has been of a durable nature and returnable to the manufacturer; (iv) since no sale is involved, the assessable article could at all enter into the determination of the value for assessment of excise duty. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The cost of secondary packing in terms of section 4(3)(d) of the Act for determining the "value" in relation to any excisable goods is only the "cost of such pack ing". [995B] 1.2 In construing section 4 (4)(a), it has to be borne in mind that the measure of excise duties is price and not value. It has to he borne in view that the legislature intended to make no change in this position, the use of the word "cost" rather than "value". [996C] 1:3 The cost for packing envisaged in section 4 is such cost incurred on account of a particular commodity to be placed in the condition in which the commodity is generally sold in the wholesale market which can be included at the factory gate which should be included In the assessable values. It is only that degree of secondary packaging which is necessary for assessable articles to be in the conditions in which they are sold in wholesale market, which can he included at a factory gate, which should he included in its assessable value if necessary by addition to the sale price except only where the cost is of a "cost", returnable to, the manufacturer.

The appellant was charged with having committed the offence of running a canteen in the State of Tamil Nadu. The prosecution case was that the appellant had taken food in the canteen for two days and being dissatisfied discontinued, stopped it. He was alleged to have pressed the demand to PW 1, who on 21.10.1975 informed him that he would help him in restoring the licence and demanded a bribe of Rs. 100. On 21. 10.1975, the appellant was stated to have made a complaint to PW I, the Chief Inspector of the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. The appellant was examined by PW 1 on 21 10 1975 itself. He had admitted that he had pressed the demands to PW l, but later on he gave the money to him. The trial court accepted the prosecution evidence and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the appellant has not been examined, the solitary evidence of PW 1 is insufficient to hold that the money was paid and there had been no demand for a bribe as there had already been no demands for a sum of Rs 100. The High Court took the view that the evidence of PWs 1 and 2 is incon sistent with the transaction of loan or return of money by PW l. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption arising under section 4(1) of Prevention of Corrup tion Act which has not be en rebutted. [337B] 1.2 In a case where the existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, there fore, the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to be rebutted. The presumption created in section 4 of the Act has not to be displaced by mere preponderance of probabilities. [340D] 1:3. In State of Rajasthan vs Mohamed Habeeb, ; , this Court observed that though the conviction under section 5 of the prevention of Corruption is to be maintained, no separate sentence need be award ed under section161 I. P.C., the presumption has to be rebut ' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to he proved when its existence is indirectly directly established, or when on the material date that finds its strength to be unreasonable. [341E F] 1 :4. In a given case, where the prosecution witnesses are unable to prove affirmatively rebutting their presumption, the court has no choice in the matter.

The respondent company was a public limited company. It had been running its flat for six months after the expiry of its employment and had been required to pay compensation for use of the premises. The company was compelled to leave the premises in the company 's flat for 6 months after its retirement and in accordance with the company "s rules, he was required to make a declaration that he was wrongfully withholding the property of the company. In view of this, the company was constrained to lodge a complaint against the petitioner under section 630 of the Act in the Court of the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, 37th Court Esplanade Bombay alleging that he had wrongfully withheld the flat in question which had been given to him for his residence during the period of his employment and thereby committed an offence punishable under section 6(1) (a) of the . The company 'was constrained to file a complaint before the Additional chief Metropolitan Magistrate. The Company Judge held that it was not necessary to make any declaration as contemplated by section 630(l)(b) of H.P. Act, 1947 and accordingly issued process under sub section (2) of section 630. The High Court also took the view that the words "any such property" in section 630 were wide enough to include past officers and employees of a company within the ambit of section 6 of the 1947 Act which provides for prosecution of an officer or employee of a Company for wrongfully withholding possession of such property. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the words 'any such properties ' in sub section 2 of section 631 must be interpreted to mean not only the present officers and employee but also to include future officers and servants of the Company; (ii) the legislature never intended to include all past officers, employees or employees of the respondent company within its ambit of Section 630(1)(b); (iii) the word 'any ' in section 6 should be interpreted as including past officers or employees. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The words 'other employees ' in subsection (l) of Section 631 must take their colour from the context in which it appears. The whole object of enacting sub section(1), namely, to provide a summary procedure for retrieving the property and to prevent abuse of the property by an officer who is permitted to use any property of a public company during his employment, wrongfully withholds possession of it after the termination of his service. [176F G] 2. The expression 'any past or present officer ' in Section 630 of H; 176A] 3. The word 'employee ' in the section means an officer of a corporation who has obtained possession of any property or of a concern in his possession knowingly applies it to purposes other than those expressed or directed in the articles and authorised by the Act.

The appellant was the founder of a Sansthan. The Sansthan was created by the name of Sakharam Maharaj at Amalner in the year 1817, and installed the deity according to religious rites. He also acquired certain properties and the same were held by him as his own property. The appellant 's case was that he was the owner of the property and that he had been using it for Darshan by the public. The Assistant Charity Commissioner by his order dated August 25, 1956, held that the Sansthan to be a public trust and not a public religious endowment. The High Court in revision set aside the order of the District Judge and restored the order passed by the Charity Commissioner. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the temple was a private property and it was also transferred to the Shishya Adhikari to maintain it as his personal property; that there was absolutely no evidence of any restriction in the matter of continuous worship by the Public or public user of the temple as a matter of right without the least interference or restriction from the temple authorities, to foster maintenance of the worship of the deity for the benefit of the Hindu public as a whole; and that the High Court had wrongly held that there were no evidence to show that the appellant was in any way concerned with the management of the Sansthan. HELD: (i) The High court was not right in giving due importance to the admission of the constituted attorneys about the nature of the endowment by the appellant. [519 B] (ii) The order passed on August 25 1956, was a document which was relied upon both by the District judge as well as the High court. It was a deed of nomination by three businessmen of Amalmer and the appellant 'was appointed as the Treasurer in order to take charge of the properties. The trust was created for the worship and maintenance of Sri Jagannath Maharaj. The temple was dedicated to the appellant for the Darshan by public. [525 C D] (iii) The appellant had been given a full picture of the working of the temples, and he was not entitled to any protection under article 19(1)(g). [521 G] (iv) The temple in its own name was recipient of land by Royal grant and the said right was taken away by the Government in favour of the Temple or the Sansthan for the purpose of maintenance of worship. [500 E] (v) The fact that the deity installed in the temple is not conclusive evidence of the restriction in question on the temple being a public temple.

The appellant was the sole proprietor of a business carried on under the name and style of Indestro Sales and Service Co. Ltd., Bombay, carrying on business in the City of Bombay. The respondent firm was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 58 by the Third Income Tax Officer, Cannanore, for the assessment year 1947 48. The appellant challenged the validity of the said assessment on the ground that section 46(2) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, under which the Income Tax officer issued a recovery certificate to the Additional Collector of Bombay was void under article 13(1) of that Constitution in that the same was repugnant to article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that section 16 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876, underwhich the warrant of arrest was issued by the Additional Collec tor of Bombay, was void and the same being repugnant to Article 14 of that Act, was not saved by article 21 of the Constitu tion. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 13 of the Act was violative of article 21 inasmuch as it offended article 22(1), and (2) that section 17 of the City Land Reve nue Act, 1889, under Which the warrant for arrest was passed by the Collector was void in that it contravened article 14. HELD: The provisions of the State laws which prescribe that machinery are not incorporated in section 46 (2), do not violate article 21. They are not in terms and by themselves, they are concerned at all with the recovery of income tax demand. [157 E] The State laws prescribe the procedure for the recovery and have to be followed in accordance with the procedure prescribed by their own State laws as if those provisions were set out in the Indian Incometax Act in extenso and it is not possible to say that all the provisions of all the State law are, mutatis mutandis, to be read into section 46. [158 E] In the present case, the appellant had been arrested and detained for a longer period than six months and was being detained for more than the period limited by the Code of Civil Procedure for the detention of a judgment debtor in execution of a decree for an equal amount of money. The State law prescribes the procedure which is followed in the exercise of its powers under article 136 of the constitution.

The respondents were the owners of a Prince 's and Victoria Docks under which each shift consisted of 8 hours ' normal duty, 2 hours ' overtime and one hour 's overtime. The Trustees agreed to accept the hours of rest at fixed hours in the Alexandra Docks but at the Prince 'S guilty of the breach of the Act and the Rules. They were prosecuted for contravening section 3(1)(a) of the , and section 13(2) read with section 5 of the . The Tribunal held that the Union was not able to establish that the existing system of work required any modification, that the so called period of rest was illusory since being variable, it was some times given right at the commencement of the shift and some times at the end. On appeal by special leave: Held, that on any single day the number of hours of work must not exceed 9 and together with the hours off rest the total period of work and rest should not go beyond 12 hours. The provisions of section 51 of the are applicable to all factories irrespective of their location or their location. The Bombay Port Trust Employees ' Union vs The Employees of the Port of Bombay, ; , referred to. The Tribunal was right in holding that the union was not entitled to fix the number and hours of working in a six day week. The workers were entitled to three hours ' wages in accordance with section 51, but they did not do so. The period of leave at the beginning of a month is not a part of the normal working day. The hours of duty are only 8 hours for any day and work up to 9 hours on any day can be taken without paying overtime if the total number of days in the week does not exceed 48. The fact that the workers were required to work beyond 9 hours in a 12 hour shift, but he must pay a double rate for any hour or part of an hour of actual work in excess of 9 hours would not make him liable to pay overtime if his total number exceeded 48.

The appellant was the tenant of a accommodation in the first floor of the building. The respondent landlord filed an application for eviction under section 13(1)(i) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 on the ground that the shop and the basement were separately let out to the appellant. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the provisions of U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 will not apply to the premises in view of the language of sections 39 and 40 of the Act. The first appellate court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the second appeal on the view that since the premises were let out in June 1976, the provisions would not apply for 10 years from October 1, 1976 and therefore the suit could be decreed as the protection available under this Act will not be available to the tenant. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the rights of parties will be governed on the basis of the date on which the suit was filed; (ii) even if the matter is pending in this Court and 10 years have elapsed since the date of the commencement of the proceedings, the appellant tenant will be entitled to protection under this section because according to him the appeal will be a continuation of the suit and therefore it would not be possible for the appellant to get the benefit of the provisions contained in section 20(2) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The rights of the parties will depend on the date when the suit is filed or from such date of commencement of this Act i.e. 15th July 1972 and therefore, it cannot be said that the present revision petition or the appeal either to the High court or the appellate authority arose out of suit which was pending on the dates on which this Act came into force.

The respondent instituted a suit for ejectment of three persons, who were the tenants under him and the third as a person who had purported to purchase the structures on the land and the tenancy right therein. The trial court held that the appellant was not liable to ejectment in view of section 3 of the Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, as amended by the West Bengal Thika Tenants (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952, which came into force on January 1, 1951. On appeal the High Court confirmed the decision of the Subordinate Judge and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (1) the respondent was not entitled to the benefit of section 4 of the Act as amended in 1953; (2) the amendment of the West Thika tenancy Act by the Amending Act of 1953, had to be examined to show how far they disturb the rights of landlord to recover possession of the property from a person, who would be a thika tenant on 28th February 1949; and (3) the High court was in error in holding that the respondent could not be said to have acquired any of the grounds mentioned in section 3. HELD: (i) The amendment of 1956 had to proceed on the basis that he was such a tenant in 1949 with the result that he could claim the benefit under section 4. [184 B] (ii) Section 5(1) of the Calcutta Thika Tenant Act, 1948, as it stood at the relevant time, provided that "the provisions of this Act shall apply to all suits and proceedings including proceedings for eviction of a thikika tenant which are pending on the date of commencement of this Ordinance. " The respondent was therefore entitled to succeed in his suit. [185 G] (iii) Section 4 of Act of 1949 was prospective only, it could not apply to pre Act suits. The landlord had to establish that he had been so a thata tenant in view Of section 3 and the only qualification was that even if the suit had been filed before the Act but was not disposed of by that date, the landlord had also to establish the existence of one of the ground specified in section 4(1). [185 B C] (iv) The High Court was right in holding on the view that sections 4 and 5 being prospective only it could apply to the case.

The State Government appointed a Pay Rationalisation Committee with wide ranging reference to the pay scale of Rs. 160 320 as against Rs.120 300 to Section Officers. The Committee recommended for approval of the pay scales of the Bench Secretaries and also recommended that the nomenclature of posts of Bench Secretaries be changed from Rs. 120 300 to Rs.200 400. The High Court suggested a uniform pay scale for all the posts of Benches of the High Court. The State Government accepted this recommendation and issued an order dated July 2, 1976 directing that all Bench Secretaries irrespective of their grades should be given the same pay scale which is being given to Superintendents i.e. Rs. 150 350. The appellant State Government filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the validity of the order of the Chief Justice. The learned Single Judge of the Allahabad High Court allowed the writ petition and directed that all Benches Secretaries irrespective on the basis of seniority alone, but on the ground that they were not entitled to the same scale of pay which was being given by Superintendents i,e. it was not open to them to have been given the similar scale of Pay as was being paid to Superintendents. The Division Bench also held that the principle of "equal pay for equal work" has to be construed in the light of Article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that the High Courts were not right in giving higher pay scale only to ten Judges and that the creation of two grades with different pay scales in the cadre of Bench Secretary who are doing the same or similar work is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The principle of equal pay for unequal work has to he construed in this first place. Functions may be the same but the responsibilities make a difference. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. So long as such value judgment emphasise that equal pay is a concomitant of Article14 of the constitution. But it follows naturally that equal pays for unequal works will be a negation of that right. [297G H] 2. The Court has completely overlooked the criterion provided under the Rules The merit governs the grant of higher pay scales and that merit will be evaluated by a competent authority. The classification made under the rules, therefore cannot be said to be violative of the right to have equal pay. After the argument was concluded in this appeal, counsel on both sides brought to our attention that the State Government has granted uniform pay scales for Bench Secretaries with effect from January 1, 1986. When Bench Secretaries Grade I acquire experience and also display more merit, they are appointed as Bench Secretaries grade I.
