The rules thus make a proper classification for the purpose of entitlement to higher pay Scale. [298H; 299A B] 3.

The appellant companies were incorporated under the . The State Government of Madhya Pradesh, in exercise of its powers under section 127A of the M.P. Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, framed a scheme for the development and administration of certain areas in the State. The scheme was published in the Gazette on June 24, 1976. The appellant companies challenged the validity of the scheme by filing writ petitions before the High Court of Madhya Bharat challenging the validity. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the scheme was not covered by the agreement of 1976 and therefore it was beyond the scope of section 127 A of the Act. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant companies it was contended that (i) since the appellant company was owned wholly by the Government of India, the lands were owned wholly and exclusively by the State Government; (ii) the provisions conferring powers of taxation under the aforesaid two Acts must be taken to have been incorporated in section 69(d) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation and the Municipal Corporation was not competent to impose the property tax; (iii) since it was not liable to pay entry tax by reason of the agreement, on January 4, 1977 respondent 1 could not impose that tax without following the procedure prescribed by sections 129 and 133 of the Municipal Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The High court was right in holding that in the instant case, subsequent amendments made to the Municipal Corpora tion Act and the Municipalities Act will also apply to the power of taxation provided for in section 127(d). [14 B] (i)(a) The object of the two Acts is to provide for the improvement and administration by providing for the proper and scientific utilisation of coal resources. The legislative field covered by Entry 23 of List II will pass on to Parliament by virtue of Entry 54, List I. But in order to 20 judge whether, on that account, the State Legislature loses its competence to pass the Act of 1973 it is necessary to have regard to the object and purpose of that Act and to the relevant provisions thereof under which Special Area Development Authorities are given the power to tax lands and buildings within their jurisdiction. [14 C D] (b) The High Courts were right in taking the view that subsequent amendments brought about by the two enactments could not be availed of by respondent 1. [15 E F] (c) The State Legislature lost its competence in entering into the agreement with the appellant Companies, under which respondent 1 bound itself not to impose any tax whatsoever. [16 G] (d) The power conferred by the Act on the Central Government to impose property tax on lands and building is not in conflict with the power conferred upon the Union Government to regulate and develop the Coal Mines so as to ensure rational and scientific utilization of coal resource. The paramount purpose behind the declaration contained in section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957 is not to control the mining industry but to impose a duty on the owner of the land or building as the case may be for the purposes of that section a tenant of land or buildings or both who holds the same under a lease for an agreed period with a convenant for its renewal thereafter. [17 E F; 18 A] (2) The first contention is without substance and must fail. The second contention is that assuming that section 127B of the , was not applicable to the case, it was open to the State to impose tax on land and buildings in accordance with the provisions thereof, under sections 129 & 133 of that Acts. [18 C] (3) The Act is primarily concerned with the development, and regulation of declared industries and not with the ownership of industrial undertakings.

The appellant was granted a lease of certain slate quarries in his estate for five years in respect of the slate quarry. The lessee applied to the Government under section 20(1) of the Abolition Act, for a renewal of the lease and on December 27, 1955, the Board of Revenue passed an order declaring that the lease should be terminated without any compensation. On December 27 the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Board. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the termination of the appellant 's leasehold rights which were created on or after July 1, 1945, could only be done under the third proviso to section 20 (1) and not under section 21(2). On appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The words "such rights" in the third Proviso to section 7(1), refer to rights created after July I, 1945 mentioned in the previous proviso. The words 'such rights ' in the second proviso have reference to rights conferred on or before the date of the first proviso and not to those which are expressly mentioned in that proviso. (ii)The third proviso is merely declaratory and does not relate to the rights mentioned in section 20 of the Act. The effect of the second Proviso is that the Government must do something to avoid them. If the third, proviso also applies to such leases as the petitioners contended, then the Government could have exercised the right conferred on it by the second, proviso and therefore, the Government was bound to give three months ' notice. (iii)The words " such rights" refer to the right created after the first July 1. 1945, mentioned in sub section (2) must be read as a proviso not to the section but to the second. The third proviso does not apply to the present case because the third and the third provisos deal with the rights created before the notified date but after July lI, 1945 for a period exceeding one year.
